briefs.title: Where Colorado's housing tax credits go: 9% and 4% awards against renter need, 2016 to 2026
briefs.takeaway: CHFA's competitive 9% tax credit reaches well beyond the Front Range: the rest of Colorado has 12% of renters paying half their income for rent and received 30% of the 9% credit from 2016 to 2026. The 4% bond credit stays on the Front Range (94% of its homes). Within regions, counties differ a lot, and 30 counties had no 9% award.
briefs.summary: This brief adds up every CHFA housing tax credit award from 2016 to 2026, 149 9% awards and 293 4% deals (171 in CHFA's rounds and 122 bond deals awarded outside them), by county and by CHFA region. It compares them with the renter households in each place that pay 50% or more of their income for rent (American Community Survey 2020-2024, table B25070; renter households are those for which Census computes rent as a share of income). All of these homes are rentals with income limits; tax credits fund no homes for sale. An index of 1.0 means a place got the same share of 9% credit as its share of those renters.
briefs.implications: For a town outside the Front Range, the 9% round is the realistic path: 4% bond deals have rarely reached a small town. Because the 2027-28 plan has no regional set-asides, each year's result depends on who applies, so a region's share swings from year to year. For anyone reading the county table: a high index is not a sign of too much housing, and a low one is not a sign of neglect. A single 50-home award moves a small county a long way, and the index does not count homes funded before 2016 or by other programs.
sources: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey

sections.heading: The short version
items: All of these homes are rentals with income limits. From 2016 to 2026, CHFA awarded the competitive 9% credit to 149 buildings with 7,743 homes, and the 4% credit, paired with tax-exempt bonds, to 293 deals with 32,666 homes. 122 of those 4% deals (14,057 homes) were bond deals CHFA awarded outside its two yearly rounds.

The 9% credit reaches well beyond the Front Range. The four Front Range regions have 88% of the renters who pay half their income or more for rent, and they received 70% of the 9% credit. The rest of Colorado has 12% of those renters and received 30%.

The 4% credit stays on the Front Range: 94% of its homes. Bond deals need enough homes to carry their fixed costs, so they rarely reach small towns. The Northeast, Upper Arkansas Valley, Southeast and San Luis Valley regions each had under 1% of them.
The Western Slope has 5.7% of these renters and received 18.5% of the 9% credit, about 3.3 times the state rate.

Counties within a region differ a lot. Mesa, the Western Slope's largest county, has 37% of the region's renters paying half their income and received 23% of its 9% credit, an index of 2.0. Montezuma is at 7.5, Garfield is at 6.8 and Delta is at 4.3.

30 of Colorado's 64 counties had no 9% award in these years, and 27 had no tax credit award at all. The largest without a 9% award are Eagle (2,195 renter households paying half or more) and San Miguel (594 renter households paying half or more).

sections.heading: The map
paragraphs: Each county is shaded by its index: its share of Colorado's 9% credit from 2016 to 2026, divided by its share of renter households paying 50% or more of income. Darker means more 9% credit for its need. Tap or hover a county for its figures.

table.caption: CHFA regions, awards 2016 to 2026. Shares are of the Colorado total. Index: share of 9% credit divided by share of renters paying 50%+ of income (1.0 = state rate).

sections.heading: Within a region
paragraphs: A region's total can hide large differences between its counties. On the Western Slope, Mesa County received 20 9% homes for every 1,000 renter households, against 32 in the rest of the region and 10 in Colorado as a whole.
Of the 28 counties with at least 500 renter households paying half their income, the highest index is Montezuma (7.5) and the lowest with any 9% award is Douglas (0.4).

table.caption: All 64 counties, largest need first. The index is left blank where fewer than 500 renter households pay 50%+ of income, because a single award swings it.

sections.heading: Over time
paragraphs: CHFA funds 12 to 16 9% buildings a year in 8 to 13 counties. The Western Slope's share of 9% homes ranged from 0% in 2025 to 35% in 2019. CHFA held its 9% round in the second round of the year until 2019 and in Round One from 2020.
Back-to-back years are uncommon outside the Front Range. Of the 41 times a county there won a 9% award, it won another the next year five times. Since 2020, only Garfield (2023 and 2024) has done it.

sections.heading: Limits of this brief
items: Counts are by county. A county total does not show which towns in it were served.
Credit amounts are the yearly amounts CHFA prints at award, added up across awards. Later exchanges or changes are not shown. Awards CHFA reports as returned are left out.

4% bond deals CHFA awarded outside its rounds are not in the round reports. They are the 122 properties on CHFA's tax credit list with a 4% award year from 2016 to 2026 that no round award accounts for, matched the same way as the site's Funding vs Need tab. They count in 4% homes, with no credit amount. CHFA's list has no award year after 2025 yet, so bond deals outside the rounds after that are not counted.
Renters paying 50% or more of income is one measure of need. It counts renters only; homeowners are not part of this comparison.
Regions are as CHFA's tax credit property list groups counties. 16 counties with no property on that list were placed with the CHFA region they border.
One 2016 award on CHFA's 9% report (Vida at St. Anthony's (4% Portion)) has no county on CHFA's report and is left out.
The index covers 2016 to 2026 only. It does not count homes funded earlier, or by Proposition 123, HOME, Division of Housing or local money.

briefs.title: Tariffs and the cost of building homes: what rose, what did not, and whether it built anything
briefs.takeaway: The metal in a building costs much more than a year ago, with tariffs of up to 50% and war-driven fuel costs both in force: steel mill products are up 32.9%, and copper, aluminum and wire roughly a fifth to a quarter (Bureau of Labor Statistics, October 2026). The price data does not show how much of that is tariffs. Cement, drywall and factory prices for appliances are flat. US steel output is up 5.9% this year, but sawmills shrank and fewer homes were started. The costs fall on rental and for-sale homes alike.
briefs.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the broad 2025 tariffs on February 20, 2026. The product tariffs that reach building materials were not part of that case and remain: 50% on steel, aluminum and copper products, 10% on softwood lumber plus 24.75% in trade duties on most Canadian lumber, and 25% on kitchen cabinets and vanities, set to double on January 1, 2027. A war in the Middle East began in late February 2026, and diesel is up 115.2% in a year. The cost of what goes into a new home is up 10.4%, and no source separates tariffs from fuel and freight in that figure.
briefs.implications: For a Colorado tax credit building: rents cannot go above a legal limit, so the part of a cost increase that rents within the limit cannot cover becomes funding gap. Wood-frame walk-ups, the usual rural building, use little structural steel; their exposure is wiring, electrical panels, heating and cooling, plumbing, metal roofing, rebar, cabinets and appliances. Plan imported cabinet orders around the January 1, 2027 increase, and treat a cost estimate older than about six months as low on metal and electrical items. Denver non-residential building costs rose 6.84% in a year on Mortenson's index, whose authors say the July 2026 tariff changes were not yet in those prices.
sources: Trade law firm and industry summaries

sections.heading: The short version
items: Metal rose most, while tariffs and war-driven fuel costs were both in force. Steel mill products are up 32.9% in a year and 52.8% since January 2025, the last month before the new tariffs. Wire, electrical panels, sheet metal and metal doors followed.
Almost nothing got cheaper. Cement, drywall, brick and factory prices for major appliances barely moved.

Lumber is the one relief. Framing lumber sold for $443.65 per thousand board feet on November 13, 2026, down 1.2% from a year earlier, and the duty on most Canadian lumber fell from 35.16% to 24.75% in October 2026.
Steel mills gained; wood and housing did not. Raw steel output is up 5.9% this year. Sawmill capacity fell 6.0%, and single-family home starts are down 4.0%.
Fuel rose at the same time. Diesel more than doubled in the year after a war began in late February 2026, which raises the cost of freight and of anything made with heat.

sections.heading: Tariffs in force on building materials
paragraphs: The broad tariffs of 2025 ended when the Supreme Court ruled against them on February 20, 2026. The ones below still apply; each row's source is listed at the end. Most were set product by product on national-security grounds, under a law known as Section 232. Canadian lumber also carries older trade duties that are reset every year.

sections.heading: What costs more
paragraphs: Each figure is the change in what US producers charge, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Producer Price Index. The index covers metal made in the US, so the rise reaches domestic metal too. It does not show why: a tariff can give US producers room to raise prices, and their own fuel and input costs rose as well. The last column is COHO's read, not a forecast from a source.

Not all of this is tariffs. Diesel is up 115.2% in a year, and the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) puts building materials without energy at 5.8% higher than a year ago. The contractors' association calls it "a double whammy of tariff- and war-induced materials cost increases."

sections.heading: What did not rise
paragraphs: Heavy materials made close to where they are used have little tariff exposure, and they barely moved. Factory prices for major appliances are flat too, even though appliances contain taxed steel. The cause is not established.

Lumber eased as demand weakened and a duty fell. Framing lumber was down 11.1% in a month by mid November 2026. In October 2026 the duty on most Canadian mills was cut from 35.16% to 24.75%. The 10% lumber tariff still sits on top, for 34.75% in all.

sections.heading: Did tariffs build anything?
paragraphs: Steel is the clearest gain and wood the clearest loss. Housing itself shrank. The data cannot show how much of that was tariffs.

sections.heading: Why prices may have risen more than production
items: Few building materials are imported. NAHB estimates that approximately 7% of the goods in a new home came from another country. Yet prices for US-made metal rose too. One possible reason is that a tariff on imports gives US producers room to raise prices. Higher fuel and input costs are another, and the price data cannot separate them.
A Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago study of the 2025 tariffs found "neither the clear employment gains that tariff proponents anticipated nor the significant job losses that critics feared."
Projects are being stopped. In a contractor survey in summer 2026, 55% of firms had a project cancelled, postponed or scaled back in six months.

Most rural Colorado tax credit buildings are wood-frame walk-ups, which use little structural steel. Their exposure is wiring, electrical panels, heating and cooling, plumbing, metal roofing, rebar, cabinets and appliances.
Denver non-residential building costs rose 6.84% in the year to mid 2026 on Mortenson's index. Its authors say the July 2026 tariff changes were "not yet reflected in second-quarter pricing."

sections.heading: Who it reaches: renters and owners
items: Renters in income-restricted homes do not pay more than their rent limit allows. The limit follows area incomes, not building cost. A building that charges less than its limit can raise rents up to it. The effect is fewer homes built for the same public money.
Buyers of new for-sale homes can see it in the price, and so can owners who remodel.
The price figures in this brief are for materials. They are the same for a rental building and a for-sale home.

sections.heading: Dates to watch
items: January 1, 2027: the tariff on kitchen cabinets and vanities doubles to 50%.
December 31, 2027: the temporary 15% rate on electrical grid equipment and some heating and cooling equipment ends.
Canadian lumber: the next yearly duty review is under way, and home builders are pressing for a new lumber agreement with Canada.
Congress: the Housing Tariff Exclusion Act would exempt many home building materials. It has been introduced, not passed.
The war: if it ends, fuel and freight could ease. The metal tariffs would stay.

sections.heading: Limits of this brief
items: No source separates how much of each price increase is tariff and how much is the fuel and freight cost of the war. This brief reports both and does not split them.
Producer price indexes track what US producers charge nationally. They are not Colorado prices and not what a builder pays after markups and delivery.
The materials share of a contract (40% to 50%) is a COHO assumption. A real bid will differ by building type.
The tariff rate now charged on finished appliances was not confirmed against the current federal product list, so this brief gives the price series only.
The Denver cost index covers non-residential building. It is used as the nearest public Colorado measure, not as an apartment cost index.
A plan to restart idled aluminum smelting in South Carolina by June 30, 2026 was announced in August 2025. This brief did not confirm it was finished.
Housing starts can fall for many reasons, such as interest rates, fuel and labor costs. The data cannot show how much was tariffs.

briefs.title: Growth and homes for local workers: how Colorado towns keep the balance
briefs.takeaway: Short-term rentals, outside investment, new businesses and state money bring money into a town, and each can also take homes from the people who work there. Colorado towns keep the balance by pairing each one with a housing tool, sized to a measured gap in homes for local workers, with renters and owners counted separately. No single tool is enough.
briefs.summary: Colorado law gives towns and counties most of what they need. HB21-1117 lets them require affordable homes in new rental projects, as long as builders can pay a fee instead. Voters in Steamboat Springs, Summit County, Crested Butte, Ouray, Aspen and other places have approved short-term rental or lodging taxes for worker housing. HB24-1175 gives a local government a right to buy older apartment buildings and existing affordable housing when they are sold, so it can keep them affordable. And from January 1, 2027, HB26-1313 ties each town's Proposition 123 target to its recent home permits and to how fast jobs are growing in its county. Breckenridge, which uses nearly every tool, has about 1,700 of its estimated 2,300 resident-occupied homes deed-restricted for local workers.
briefs.implications: For a town, the useful question is not whether growth is good but who it houses. A linkage fee or mitigation rule mostly pays for rental homes for the lower-wage workers new businesses hire. Buying deed restrictions on existing homes mostly helps owners and buyers near or above the area median income. Proposition 123 money reaches renters at or below 60% of area median income and buyers at or below 100%. A town that uses only one tool leaves someone out. Fees also have limits: Breckenridge's rule for new businesses produced two homes in five years, and the council moved to narrow it in February 2026. Rates, caps and program terms change often, so check each one with the town before relying on it.

sections.heading: Match each source of growth with a housing tool
paragraphs: Each of these brings money into a town: visitor spending, jobs, investment and public funding. Each row says what it can cost the people who work there and the tool Colorado places use to answer it. The sections below give the examples.

table.caption: Sources of growth and the housing tool that answers each one
rows: Homes renters lived in become visitor lodging
Short-term rental or lodging tax for housing; caps in neighborhoods where locals live (renters, and owners where the money funds buy-downs)
New jobs, many at lower wages, with no homes to match
Linkage fee or housing mitigation on new commercial space (renters)
New homes priced above what local workers earn
Inclusionary housing, with a fee as the alternative (renters and buyers)
Bidding against first-time buyers; rent pressure when older buildings change hands
Local right to buy older apartments; federal limit on large buyers of single-family homes from 2027; for-cause eviction (renters and first-time buyers)
Help that may not reach local workers or the lowest incomes
Income limits and long restrictions that come with the money; local commitments (renters and buyers, by income)
Fewer homes left for year-round residents
Buying deed restrictions on existing homes; land trusts and public land (owners and buyers; land banks can also serve renters)

sections.heading: Start with the local jobs-and-homes balance
paragraphs: A fee or tax is fairest when it is tied to a measured need. The first step is one table for the town or county: for each income level, how many local workers there are, and how many homes they can afford and actually get. Count renters and owners separately, because the tools that help each are different.

Most towns are building this now. Under SB24-174, a city, town or county of 1,000 people or more (for a county, only its unincorporated residents count) must send a housing needs assessment to DOLA by December 31, 2026, on its own or through a regional assessment. A place that lost at least 1% of its population in the last census is exempt. Housing action plans are due by January 1, 2028 from places of 5,000 or more, and from places of 1,000 or more that joined a regional assessment or count as rural resort communities.

The state now links housing to jobs too. HB26-1313, approved May 26, 2026, changes the Proposition 123 commitment from 2027. A town's target becomes its average yearly home permits over the past three years, times the years it commits to, times 10%, 15% or 20%, depending on whether job growth in its county is well below, close to or well above the statewide median. Until then the commitment is a 3% annual increase in affordable homes.
items: Jobs by wage, and where those workers live: Census commuting data (LEHD) and state wage data. Many low-wage in-commuters signal a hidden gap.
Households by income, renters and owners: HUD CHAS tables, which also count the rental homes that are affordable and available to each income level.
Homes for sale: the income needed to buy a typical home, compared with what local workers earn.

The gap at each income level then sets the dial. A large gap below 60% of area median income points to rental tools and state money. A large gap near or above the area median income points to ownership tools such as deed-restriction buy-downs and land trusts.

sections.heading: Fit the tools to the place
paragraphs: The same tool can work well in one town and do little in the next. Fees on new building only raise money where building happens, so a town that is barely growing, or has no room to grow, needs a different mix from a fast-growing one. Four things tell a town which kind it is: how many homes it has permitted in recent years, how fast jobs are growing in its county compared with the state, how much buildable land is left inside or next to it, and how many of its workers live somewhere else.

The state already sizes Proposition 123 this way. From 2027 a town's target is built from its own recent home permits and its county's job growth, so a town that builds little gets a smaller target, and one that is adding jobs quickly gets a larger one.

table.caption: Which tools fit which kind of place
rows: Growing, with land to build on
Linkage fees and inclusionary housing, set from a nexus study; housing conditions when land is annexed; land banking ahead of growth
Buy-downs alone, which cannot keep pace with new jobs
Fixing and keeping the homes it has; buying deed restrictions; the right to buy older apartments; a regional housing authority shared with neighbors; holding land for later
Linkage fees and inclusionary rules, which raise little when little is built and can stop the few projects that come
Land-locked (public land, steep ground or water limits all around)

More homes on the land it has: infill, accessory dwellings, converting buildings, homes on land owned by school districts, housing authorities and other public owners; Forest Service site leases; buy-downs and short-term rental caps that keep existing homes for locals; working with the towns where its workers live
Annexation and large new subdivisions; fees that assume steady new building
Resort town with many second homes
Short-term rental and lodging taxes; neighborhood caps; buy-downs that keep existing homes for local workers
Rental-only tools that leave out workers who want to buy
Bedroom town where many residents work elsewhere
Regional agreements, so the towns where the jobs are help pay; keeping homes affordable for the renters and owners already there
A local linkage fee, since the jobs that create the need are in another town

items: In a land-locked town the gap often has to be met partly by its neighbors. Count the workers who commute in, and agree with the towns they live in on who builds and who pays.

A small or slow-growing town should be careful with fees. Breckenridge, a busy resort town, still found its rule for new businesses produced two homes in five years and stopped some businesses from opening.
Accessory dwellings are allowed wherever single-family homes are allowed in the places HB24-1152 covers, which helps towns with little open land add homes without new subdivisions.

sections.heading: Linkage fees and housing mitigation
paragraphs: A linkage fee charges new commercial space (and sometimes small homes) for the housing need its jobs create. Mountain towns often use a stronger version that requires housing for a share of the workers a project brings. Both mainly pay for rental homes for lower-wage workers. These are the linkage fees on record in this site's local housing funds data:

table.caption: Linkage fees on record
rows: Denver charges an affordable housing linkage fee per square foot of new floor area, phased up to $5.00 (small dwellings) through $9.00 (commercial uses in high market areas) by July 2025 and indexed to CPI from July 2026; residential projects may instead comply with mandatory affordable housing.

Boulder's capital facility impact fee includes an affordable housing (commercial linkage) component of $36.64 per square foot for office, $24.43 for retail/restaurant and hospital, $21.37 light industrial and $12.21 institutional/warehousing, plus $11 per square foot on large single-unit expansions and replacements.

The same voter-approved 5A measure authorizes an affordable-housing Development Impact Fee of two dollars or less per square foot on new construction and additions, which owners may avoid by voluntarily imposing a private transfer fee on later sales.

Gunnison County's 2006 Essential Housing linkage amendment imposes a Workforce Housing Fee on new residential, commercial and industrial construction (and residential additions over 500 sq ft) in unincorporated areas, based on employees generated.

items: Vail: each new or redeveloped commercial project must provide employee housing for 20% of the employees it generates, under the town code.

Breckenridge: since 2020, new businesses must house about 35% of the staff they are expected to add, by building, buying or paying a fee. In five years it produced two homes and one fee of about $43,000. On February 10, 2026 the council agreed to change the rule, starting with businesses that move into existing space.

Pitkin County: since 2020 its Employee Housing Impact Fee charges home building for the workers it creates. On April 30, 2026 the Court of Appeals upheld a fee of nearly $950,000 on a home that was torn down and rebuilt.
The lesson: a fee set from a nexus study, and kept well below what a business can bear, raises money; one set too high stops the project it was meant to charge.

sections.heading: Short-term rental taxes and neighborhood caps
paragraphs: Voters across the mountains have taxed short-term rentals and lodging to pay for worker housing, and some places cap how many homes can be rented to visitors. These are the lodging and short-term rental taxes on record in this site's local housing funds data:

table.caption: Lodging and short-term rental taxes on record
rows: Summit County voters passed Referred Measure 1A in 2022 authorizing a short-term rental lodging tax for local-worker housing and childcare; the county lists a 2% lodging tax in unincorporated Summit County effective January 1, 2023.

Frisco voters approved Ballot Question 2A on April 5, 2022 (539 to 301, unofficial), a new 5% excise tax on short-term rentals effective June 1, 2022, spent solely on affordable housing; it does not apply to hotels and motels.
Vail Ballot Issue 2A (November 2025), a proposed 6% excise tax on short-term rentals for workforce housing, was defeated 916 to 881.

Eagle County Ballot Issue 1A (2022) created a 2% lodging excise tax on stays under 30 days in unincorporated Eagle County and Gypsum, with 90% for local-workforce childcare and affordable housing and 10% for tourism marketing. Voters added another 2% in 2025, for 4% total; the county describes the support that increase funds as childcare and public safety, so it is not counted as housing money.

Aspen's voter-approved short-term rental tax (Resolution 106-2022) charges 5% on owner-occupied and lodge-exempt STRs and 10% on investment/second-home STRs for stays from May 1, 2023, with at least 70% of receipts required for community affordable housing.

Telluride voters approved Ballot Issue 300 in November 2019, a citizen-initiated 2.5% short-term rental tax for the town's Affordable Housing Fund that excludes hotel rooms; it took effect in January 2020.

Steamboat Springs voters approved a 9% short-term rental tax in November 2022, effective January 1, 2023, restricted to increasing affordable and attainable housing; the Short-Term Rental Tax Fund is projected to end 2026 with a $52.6M reserve.

Crested Butte voters passed Ballot Initiative 2D on November 2, 2021, a 7.5% excise tax on vacation and short-term rentals from January 1, 2022, dedicated to the Affordable Housing Fund and barred from general operations.
Avon dedicates its 2% short-term rental excise tax to the Community Housing Fund.

Durango 2022 Ballot Question 2A let the city keep 2021-2022 lodgers' tax revenue above estimates from the 3.25% increase and spend it 66% on affordable and workforce housing programs; CHFA lists it as passed.
La Plata County voters passed Ballot Issue 1A in November 2024, allowing revenue from the county's existing lodging tax to support workforce housing and other community improvements.

Glenwood Springs voters approved Ballot Measure 2C in 2022, a 2.5% accommodations tax on stays under 30 days (hotels, motels and short-term rentals) deposited in a dedicated Workforce Housing Fund and set to end in fiscal year 2042.

Fruita's 6% lodging tax applies to hotels and vacation rentals. Half goes to marketing; the other 3% goes to Economic Development and Public Places, whose listed uses include attainable housing. No share is set aside for housing by law, but the city has used this money for housing: $325,000 of the $400,000 it put into The Oaks redevelopment in its 2025 budget came from lodging tax.

Montrose voters approved Ballot Issue 2A in November 2024 (5,941 to 5,698), raising the city hotel room tax from 0.9% to 6% from January 1, 2025, with 33% of the tax set aside for incentives for affordable housing.

items: Steamboat Springs: voters dedicated 75% of the 9% short-term rental tax to Brown Ranch, a plan for 2,264 homes, but rejected its annexation in March 2024, 2,903 to 2,094. The city still collected an estimated $14.8 million from the tax in 2024 and gave $5 million to the Yampa Valley Housing Authority's Cottonwoods project for affordable homeownership.
Summit County: on February 15, 2023 commissioners capped short-term rental licenses outside towns by basin: 18% for Upper Blue, 15% for Lower Blue, 6% for Ten Mile and 5% for Snake River.
Crested Butte caps short-term rentals at 30% of local housing, 212 rentals. Ouray caps them at 120 and has a 15% tax, half for housing.

HB25-1247 lets county voters raise the lodging tax in unincorporated areas from 2% up to 6%. In November 2025, increases passed in Eagle, Gilpin, Hinsdale, Ouray, Routt and Park counties and failed in Chaffee and Custer. Eagle County took housing out of its measure to put childcare first, so a housing share has to be written into the ballot question or it can drop out.

sections.heading: Affordable homes in new projects (inclusionary housing)
paragraphs: HB21-1117 lets local governments require affordable units in new rental projects, and builders must be offered a fee in lieu as an alternative. These rules reach both renters and buyers.
items: Denver: new market-rate projects of ten or more homes include affordable homes on site. For rentals, 8% at 60% AMI in typical markets and 10% in high markets; for ownership, 8% or 10% at 80% AMI. Other options trade a higher share for a higher average income limit.
Boulder: 25% of homes in projects of five or more, and 20% in smaller ones, must be permanently affordable.
Longmont: 12% of new homes, affordable to buyers at or below 80% AMI and renters at or below 50% AMI.
Glenwood Springs: 20% of new homes meet community housing standards and 10% are leased or sold at 100% of area median income.
Superior: 15% of projects of 10 or more homes, at 80% of area median income.

table.caption: Fees in lieu of affordable homes on record
rows: Under Expanding Housing Affordability, Denver developers may pay a fee in lieu per required income-restricted unit ($311,000 rental / $478,000 ownership in high market areas; $250,000-$408,000 in typical areas) into the Mandatory Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund.
Boulder developers may satisfy inclusionary housing by paying cash-in-lieu into the Affordable Housing Fund, at a per-square-foot rate the city manager sets and may escalate each January 1.

Longmont lets developers meet its 12 percent inclusionary requirement by paying a fee in lieu into the Affordable Housing Fund, currently $13.50 per square foot of finished for-sale housing and $5.93 for rental, recalculated every three years.

sections.heading: Conditions on state money
paragraphs: Proposition 123 money comes with conditions. Rental homes must be affordable at or below 60% of area median income and buyer homes at or below 100%, each costing the household less than 30% of its income. To be eligible, a town files a commitment to grow its affordable homes. In the first cycle, 217 local governments filed commitments for 22,988 homes, and 156 had filed for 2027 to 2029 by the November 1, 2026 deadline.

A town can add its own conditions to the money it controls: a preference for people who work locally, long or permanent deed restrictions, and a share of homes at the income levels where its own gap is largest. This brief found no Colorado housing program that ties funding to construction wages or local hiring; that option is not confirmed here.

sections.heading: Buying deed restrictions on existing homes
paragraphs: The town pays an owner or buyer to record a permanent restriction: usually that someone who works locally must live there, and sometimes a cap on the resale price. In resort markets it is often the fastest way to keep homes for local workers, and it mainly helps owners and buyers. Vail InDEED, for example, has funded restrictions on 178 homes for $13,064,618 toward a goal of 1,000 by 2027, requiring occupants who work at least 30 hours a week in Eagle County. These are the deed-restriction programs on record:

table.caption: Deed-restriction and buy-down programs on record
rows: Through Housing Helps, Summit County pays buyers 10%-25% of a home's value to record a local-worker deed restriction on a market-rate home: 10-15% for a light restriction, 15-25% for one with a 3% annual appreciation cap; the money is not a loan.

Breckenridge's Housing Helps program, created by Resolution 17 (Series 2019), pays owners, buyers and local businesses 15-25% for a deed restriction on unrestricted homes: 15% for a light work-requirement restriction, 20-25% for a full restriction with a 3% appreciation cap.

Frisco's Housing Helps program (framework set by Resolution 19-31, August 2019) pays buyers and owners for deed restrictions on unrestricted homes and funds town buy-downs, using voter-approved 5A funds and the 5% STR excise tax.

Vail InDEED, begun in 2017, pays homeowners and buyers for a perpetual deed restriction requiring occupancy by people working in Eagle County; per Vail Daily the town provides 20% of market value with no income or appreciation caps.

Under Good Deeds Vail (2026), the Town of Vail and the Eagle County Housing and Development Authority each contribute up to 15% of a home's price (max $1.25 million) for a combined buy-down of up to 30%, capped at $375,000, in exchange for a price-capped deed restriction.

Eagle County Good Deeds (since 2021, run by the Eagle County Housing and Development Authority) pays 15% of the purchase price, up to $187,500, for a perpetual price-capped deed restriction on open-market homes up to $1,250,000; ECHDA added $2.5 million in 2026 after its initial $4 million budget was nearly depleted.

Mi Casa Avon pays home buyers a 12% match, up to $150,000, for a perpetual resident-occupied deed restriction limiting ownership and use to full-time Eagle County employees, with no appreciation cap; 56 units were added from 2020 to 2025.

Good Deeds Avon pays 30% of the purchase price, capped at $375,000 (15% from the Town, 15% from ECHDA), on homes up to $1,250,000 in exchange for a price-capped deed restriction with 0-3% annual appreciation.

sections.heading: Land trusts and public land
paragraphs: When land is held for housing for good, the public help stays with the home instead of going to the first owner who sells. This mainly serves buyers and renters at moderate incomes. Land on record in this site's data:

table.caption: Land banks and public land for housing on record
rows: Fort Collins's land bank buys land near transit, schools, parks, jobs and shopping, paid from the Affordable Housing Fund or General Fund, and sells it only to housing providers bound to build rentals for households at or below 60 percent of AMI or ownership homes at or below 80 percent.
Grand Junction is buying the 21.45-acre Salt Flats site for future affordable and attainable housing; the $3.2 million purchase is supported by a $2.2 million state Prop 123 land banking grant.

sections.heading: Guardrails on investors
items: Right to buy older apartments: under HB24-1175, approved May 30, 2024, the local government has a right of first refusal, with a matched offer, when existing affordable housing of five or more units is sold, and a right of first offer on other rental buildings of 15 to 100 units, to keep them affordable. Both rights end December 31, 2029. Adams County kept its right of first offer under the state's 2024 Rights to Property for Affordable Housing law and assigned its right of first refusal for unincorporated properties to Maiker Housing Partners.

Federal limit on large buyers: the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law on July 11, 2026. From January 7, 2027, 180 days later, an investor controlling 350 or more single-family homes will not be allowed to buy more, with exceptions such as newly built homes. Build-to-rent investment stays open.
Renters already housed: HB24-1098, approved April 19, 2024, requires a landlord to have cause to evict.

How big is corporate ownership? A state task force counted 49,278 corporate-owned homes in 2023 in the 17 counties with 90% of Colorado's homes, about 3% of homes that owners could live in. Eagle County had the highest share.

sections.heading: Keeping it fair
items: Serve each income level where the gap is. Rental tools reach the lowest incomes; buy-downs and land trusts mostly reach households near or above the median. A package that funds only ownership leaves most renters out.
Report results for renters and owners separately, never as one count.
Prefer people who work locally, not only low incomes. Occupancy rules such as Vail's keep homes for the workforce. Review any preference rule for fair housing before adopting it.
Protect people already housed. New taxes and fees pay for new homes; the right to buy older apartments and for-cause eviction protect renters who live there now.

Track each year: homes funded and preserved by tool, renters and owners, income levels served, how many occupants work locally, and money raised against the measured gap. Breckenridge raises over $13 million a year for housing and a 2023 study still found it needs about 1,200 more homes for its workforce.

sections.heading: What this brief does not show
items: It does not rank towns or score whether a package is enough; that depends on each place's own gap.
It does not list every Colorado program. The tables show what is on record in this site's local housing funds data, and "not on record" is not proof a place has none.
Fee rates, caps and program terms change often; check the current terms with the town.
Outcomes still open: the San Miguel County employee housing fee appeal and a 2025 lawsuit over Denver's affordable housing rules. This brief does not report how they end.

briefs.title: CHFA 2026 Round Two tax credit awards: who won, where, and who did not
briefs.takeaway: Colorado's housing finance agency (CHFA) reserved federal 4% and state housing tax credits for nine of 26 applications on November 16, 2026: 845 new rental homes, 8 of the 9 buildings in metro Denver. State credit was the limit, and no rural project won.
briefs.summary: CHFA says the nine developments will support the new construction of 845 affordable rental units and raise more than $234 million in private equity. CHFA's award report lists the yearly credits: $19,668,117 in federal 4% credit, $11,700,000 in accelerated state credit, $4,200,000 in standard state credit and $774,000 in Transit-Oriented Communities credit, with $146,387,212 in private activity bonds. All 845 homes are rentals with income limits; this round funds no homes for sale.
briefs.implications: Expect a crowded 2027 Round Two: 17 applications with 1,882 homes missed this year, and five of this year's nine winners had missed in 2025 and come back. Plan the gap around the state credit cap, show local backing early, and expect smaller buildings with deep income targeting and named services to compete best. Round Two did not reach a small town this year; for a rural 4% deal, size and gap money need solving before applying.

sections.heading: The short version
items: Nine of 26 applications won. CHFA reserved federal 4% and Colorado state housing tax credits for nine new rental buildings with 845 homes, all with income limits for renters. 17 applications with 1,882 rental homes did not get credits this round.
State credit was the limit. Every winner got the full $1.3M accelerated state credit. CHFA awarded $11.7M of the $33.8M in accelerated state credit that applicants asked for, about 35%.

Eight of nine are in metro Denver (783 homes). The other is 62 homes for older adults and veterans leaving homelessness in Grand Junction. No rural or mountain project won; the only rural application, in Cortez, did not.
53% of the homes (450) are for renters at or below 50% of area median income (AMI), and 17% (141) are at 30%. The average is about 52% AMI.
Five of the nine winners had applied in 2025 Round Two and not won. Housing authorities and nonprofits sponsored seven of the nine.

briefs.title: Forest Service land leases for housing: what the December 2 rule changes and which Colorado counties could use it
briefs.takeaway: From December 2, 2026, a lease of a Forest Service administrative site can back a loan. A final rule takes these leases out of the special-use rules that let the Forest Service end a lease on its own and kept lenders away. The window is short: the law lets the Forest Service sign new leases only until October 1, 2028. In Colorado, Summit and Routt counties have already tried and stalled over financing, and eight more mountain counties have offices in town, commuting workers and renters short of homes.
briefs.summary: The final rule, Administrative Site Leases (91 FR 68887), was published November 2, 2026 and takes effect December 2, 2026. It moves leases of Forest Service administrative sites (ranger stations, work centers, old dwellings and the land around them) out of the special-use permit rules. Under those rules a lease could not serve as loan collateral, could not readily be assigned, and could be ended by the Forest Service on its own, and the rule says those terms "limit financing options." The housing power itself comes from section 8623 of the 2018 Farm Bill: leases of up to 100 years and up to 40 acres, offered first to the town or county, with rent paid in cash or in housing for Forest Service staff. Colorado has the first lease signed under that law, Summit County's Dillon Work Center (September 27, 2023), and its housing has not been built.
briefs.implications: For a town or county with a Forest Service office or work center, the first step is to ask the forest supervisor whether the site is on the regional forester's list, because the town or county gets the first offer. A lender can now take the leasehold as collateral, so a tax-credit or locally funded rental project can be financed the usual way, subject to each lease's terms. Leave time: a site needs an appraisal, NEPA review and public notice, and new leases must be signed before October 1, 2028. Check with counsel whether the statute's bar on federal cash payments reaches rental assistance before counting on vouchers.

sections.heading: What the rule changes
paragraphs: The rule removes administrative site leases from the Forest Service's special-use regulations (36 CFR 251.50 and 251.51). It covers leases under the 2018 Farm Bill (Pub. L. 115-334, sec. 8623) and the 2005 Forest Service Facility Realignment and Enhancement Act (Pub. L. 109-54). It was adopted unchanged from the May 6, 2026 proposal after 25 comments: 8 for, 17 against.

Under the old rules a lease could not serve as loan collateral, could not easily be assigned, and could be ended by the Forest Service on its own. The rule says those terms "limit financing options." Lender step-in and default terms now go in each lease.

What it does not do: it does not authorize land sales, and leases still need NEPA review, historic-preservation review, public notice and local consultation. A loan against the lease does not touch the federal title to the land. Existing permits stay as written unless both sides agree to replace them with a lease.

sections.heading: What the law allows
paragraphs: The housing power is in the statute, not the rule. Section 8623, as the EXPLORE Act amended it in January 2025, sets these terms:
items: What can be leased: a ranger station, work center, dwelling or other administrative site and the land under or next to it, plus no more than 10 isolated, undeveloped parcels of 40 acres or less each fiscal year, nationwide. Wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, national monuments and land set aside for recreation are excluded.
Size: one lease may not exceed 40 acres.

Term: not more than 100 years. Each lease must allow the use to be reauthorized, possibly on new terms, if the site is still used as authorized, the new use fits the forest's land management plan and the lessee has kept to the lease. Renewal is not automatic. Before 2025 the statute set no term; the 2023 Dillon lease runs 50 years.
First offer: the Forest Service must offer the lease to the town or county where the site is before anyone else.
Rent: at least market value, in cash or in kind. In-kind rent can be new facilities "such as housing" for Forest Service staff.
Local rules: the lessee follows state and local zoning, building codes and permits.
Who picks sites: a regional forester recommends the sites in the region that can be leased.

sections.heading: The deadline: October 1, 2028
paragraphs: The authority to sign new leases under section 8623 expires October 1, 2028; leases signed before then stand. It lapsed once before, on October 1, 2023, and stalled the Steamboat Springs project until Congress restored it in January 2025.

The second authority, the 2005 act, was extended through September 30, 2026 by the 2026 appropriations act. This brief has not confirmed whether the current stopgap funding law carries it past that date, so treat it as unconfirmed.

sections.heading: Where Colorado has tried it
paragraphs: Summit County signed the first lease under the law on September 27, 2023: 50 years for the 11-acre Dillon Work Center, for up to 177 rental homes, with rent paid in housing for Forest Service staff. Most units are for Summit County workers and residents who qualify. A 162-unit plan at 80% to 120% of area median income fell through last year over financing, and the county is now in talks with a new developer.

In Steamboat Springs, the Yampa Valley Housing Authority worked for years on an 8-acre site on Hilltop Parkway for up to 84 apartments at 50% to 140% of area median income. The city manager said the inability to solve the leasing issues proved "fatal" to the project. Eagle and Pitkin counties explored leases in 2024 but did not sign one.

sections.heading: Colorado counties that could use it
paragraphs: 46 of Colorado's 64 counties hold national forest land, 41 have a Forest Service office or work center, and 66 of the state's 272 towns and cities have national forest land within a mile of their center. The table lists the counties where a lease has been tried or explored, then the counties where this site's own data shows the clearest fit: a Forest Service office in a town, workers commuting in, and renters without an affordable home. It is a screen, not a ranking. Apart from Summit County's signed Dillon lease, no site in it is known to have been offered for lease.
Every project on record is rental housing: the land stays federal and the homes are rented. Nothing on record uses these leases for homes people own.

sections.heading: Counties left off the table, and why
items: Front Range counties (Larimer, Boulder, Jefferson, El Paso, Douglas) have the largest measured need, but their Forest Service offices sit in cities with other public and private land. Fort Collins has a named Forest Service administrative site.
Mineral, Hinsdale, San Juan, Jackson and Rio Blanco are mostly forest but show little measured need for worker or renter housing.
San Miguel's only Forest Service office is in Norwood, far from the Telluride jobs, and the county is dropped from the boost-area list for 2027.

sections.heading: Open questions before anyone signs
items: Rental help: the statute says no federal agency "shall make any cash payments relating to the use or occupancy" of a site improved or constructed under it. Read plainly, that could reach housing vouchers or USDA rental assistance in these homes. The rule does not address it. Ask counsel before counting on rental assistance.

Tax credits need a long lease: CHFA's 2027-2028 plan scores 15 years of compliance plus 25 years of extended use, and does not count a letter of intent as site control. A lease of 50 to 100 years can cover that; any lender's own minimum term is not checked here.
An office is not an offer: the office list includes buildings the Forest Service rents from others, and only a regional forester can recommend a site.
Forest land near a town is a lead, not a site: the isolated-parcel route allows only 10 parcels a year, nationwide.

Distances are from each town's center point, so a town with forest at its edge can be missed.

briefs.title: Vacancy taxes in Colorado: who can levy one, Boulder's 2J, and what it could raise
briefs.takeaway: Colorado has no state law that lets every town tax empty homes: HB26-1036, which would have, died in committee on February 9, 2026. Home-rule cities and towns can still ask their own voters, and Boulder's did on November 3, 2026, by passing 2J, a tax on homes occupied 183 days or less a year. The owners of empty homes pay it; renters do not.
briefs.summary: Boulder voters passed Ballot Issue 2J with 58% in unofficial results. It charges the owner $4,000 a year for a home occupied 183 days or less, rising with inflation but never above $7,000, starting January 1, 2028. The money goes to general city services, not housing. Steamboat Springs drafted a $3,100 tax in 2025, but its council voted 4-3 not to send it to voters. Crested Butte voters turned down a housing tax on non-primary homes in 2021, 448 to 344, and a second version, 2B, was failing in the November 2026 unofficial count. Below, COHO estimates what a tax at Boulder's rate could raise in each home-rule town, using Census counts of second homes and other vacant homes.
briefs.implications: For a town: only a home-rule municipality can levy a vacancy tax today, and only after a TABOR election. A statutory town would have to adopt a home-rule charter first. If the money should go to housing, the ballot question has to say so; Boulder's does not. A tax that works shrinks its own base as owners rent or sell, so it is a shaky base for long-term debt. For renters: the tax falls on owners, and a home with a long-term tenant counts as occupied. Its housing effect is homes coming back onto the rental market. For owners: heirs, owners renovating and older owners in care are in the same Census count as second-home owners, so the exemptions decide who pays.
sources: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey

sections.heading: What Colorado law allows
items: HB26-1036 would have let counties and municipalities tax vacant homes with voter approval, short-term rentals excluded, and limited the money to affordable, attainable or workforce housing. The House Finance Committee voted 7-4 against it, and it was postponed indefinitely on February 9, 2026.

Home-rule cities and towns hold the power to levy taxes for municipal purposes under Article XX, Section 6 of the Colorado Constitution, so they can ask their voters for a vacancy excise tax without a state law. Boulder did. The Crested Butte News reported that, as a home-rule town, Crested Butte already has the authority.
Statutory towns, statutory cities and counties hold only the powers a statute grants, and no statute grants this one. A statutory town can adopt a home-rule charter first.

TABOR requires voter approval in advance, decided at a state general election, a biennial local district election or a November election in an odd-numbered year; a ballot title that opens "Shall (district) taxes be increased," and voter approval to keep money above the revenue limit or to repay debt from the tax. It bans new real estate transfer taxes, so a vacancy tax cannot be built as one.
Property taxes must be uniform within a class (Article X, Section 3), so a local vacancy tax is written as an excise tax. No Colorado court has ruled on whether that holds.

sections.heading: How the estimate works
paragraphs: Revenue equals second homes times the share that would owe, plus other vacant homes times the share that would owe, times the share collected, times the rate. The shares below are COHO assumptions, not published research: some second homes are lived in more than half the year, rented long term part of the year or used as short-term rentals; much of the other vacant count is what hardship exemptions cover; and owners respond by renting, selling or proving occupancy.

Two local checks support the middle case. In Boulder, before collection, it counts about as many owing homes as the city's water-use count of about 500 single-family homes vacant more than six months. In Steamboat Springs, at the city's $3,100 rate, it lands inside the city staff's range.

sections.heading: Who it reaches: renters and owners
items: Renters pay nothing directly. A home with a long-term tenant counts as occupied, so the tax applies only while a home sits empty.
If owners rent rather than pay, more homes come onto the rental market. That is the tax's main housing effect, separate from where the money goes.
A landlord whose unit sits empty more than half the year between tenants would owe the tax unless an exemption covers it. Boulder's 2027 ordinance will decide this.
Second-home owners are the main target, and many cannot vote in the town that taxes them.
Heirs, owners renovating and older owners in care fall into the Census other vacant count. Without hardship exemptions they would pay too.

sections.heading: Limits of this brief
items: ACS counts a home as vacant on the day it was surveyed. A home lived in four months a year can be counted as occupied, so ACS is a cautious base for a 183-day test.
Small-town seasonal counts carry wide margins of error; treat their dollars as an order of magnitude.
Short-term rentals are counted as taxable. A town that exempts them, as HB26-1036 would have, has a smaller base; official license counts are on record here only for a few towns.

Municipal types (home rule or statutory) are from the Wikipedia list of Colorado municipalities, which cites DOLA; DOLA's own list could not be opened from COHO's tools. Check a town's charter before relying on its status.

No Colorado court has ruled on whether a vacancy excise tax is a non-uniform property tax.
Boulder's exemptions, proof of occupancy and enforcement are not set until a 2027 ordinance.

briefs.title: 2026 midterms: Democrats projected to win Congress (unofficial); what it means for affordable housing in Colorado
briefs.summary: Unofficial results as of November 4, 2026. Democrats are projected to win control of both the U.S. House and Senate, according to AP projections reported by Realtor.com and NBC News; the new majorities take office with the 120th Congress in January 2027. In Colorado, Sen. John Hickenlooper (D) was re-elected with 60.2% on the Secretary of State's election night count (updated 4:02 AM MST, 25 of 64 counties fully reported). CPR News reported that Manny Rutinel (D) flipped the 8th District (55.5% to Rep. Gabe Evans' 40.8%). The 3rd District (Rep. Jeff Hurd 48.6%, Dwayne Romero 48.2%) and 4th District (Eileen Laubacher 49.2%, Rep. Lauren Boebert 47.7%) were uncalled; Jessica Killin (D) led the 5th District 51.6% to Rep. Jeff Crank's 45.3%. Housing positions on record: Hickenlooper says he fought to include in the ROAD to Housing Act a limit on large institutional investors buying more than 350 single-family homes and permanent grants for manufactured housing communities (PRICE Act). Sen. Michael Bennet, not on the ballot, co-leads the More Homes on the Market Act with Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), which would double the home-sale capital gains exclusion to $500,000 for single filers and $1 million for joint filers. Killin told KRDO she would lower housing costs "by creating incentives that will increase supply, especially entry-level housing." Rutinel's campaign pledges to "make housing more affordable" without a specific federal proposal. No specific housing plan was found in the sources COHO could open for Hurd, Romero, Laubacher or Boebert. Rep. Brittany Pettersen's Housing Supply Frameworks Act (HUD zoning best-practice frameworks), Streamlining Rural Housing Act (one HUD-USDA review) and VALID Act became part of the ROAD to Housing Act. Rep. Joe Neguse reintroduced the Save Affordable Housing Act as H.R. 4572 in 2025; it would end the LIHTC qualified-contract option for future developments and base the purchase price for existing properties on their value as affordable housing. His Housing Fairness for Mountain Communities Act, which would let areas set area median income by ZIP code or region instead of county, was introduced in 2023; COHO has not confirmed a version in the current Congress. Rep. Jeff Crank's office reported on May 20, 2026 that he voted for the House version of the ROAD to Housing package, citing lower regulatory costs for manufactured homes and veterans' access to housing assistance. No housing release was found from Reps. Hurd, Boebert or Evans in the sources COHO checked. The White House says President Trump has been "laser-focused on making housing more affordable"; his Executive Order 14376 of January 20, 2026 directs federal agencies and the GSEs not to help large institutional investors buy single-family homes that families could buy, with exceptions for build-to-rent. The administration also signals vetoes of Democratic bills. Nationally, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become Speaker, said on October 21 that Democrats "need to dramatically build more housing that the American people can afford" and called to "enhance and strengthen the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit"; his affordability agenda includes a housing working group (Reps. Emilia Sykes and Laura Friedman) on rents, homeownership, construction red tape, renter protections and homelessness, which had not released bills. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer's "Opportunity Starts at Home" plan (January 15) would expand Section 8 and emergency vouchers, target rent-setting algorithms, add down-payment help, remove rules that block building, create a public housing fund and use the Defense Production Act for modular homes.
briefs.implications: What is already law does not change with the election: Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025) permanently raised each state's 9% housing credit ceiling by 12% and lowered the tax-exempt bond test from 50% to 25%, and Public Law 119-101, the ROAD to Housing Act (July 11, 2026), reformed HUD and supply programs but authorizes no new appropriations (section 1202). The first money decision belongs to the outgoing Congress. Federal funding runs on a continuing resolution through December 11, 2026. NLIHC reports that the House FY27 HUD bill would cut HUD programs about 8% and that the Senate bill had not been released; Congress returns November 9. Colorado's HOME, CDBG, voucher and Continuum of Care funding for 2027 will be set in that lame-duck session or in another stopgap that carries into the new Congress. Leaning: both parties ran on housing costs, and the federal housing laws of 2025 and 2026 passed with support from both. A Democratic Congress is more likely to resist HUD cuts in FY28 and to move bills still in committee, such as the roughly two dozen unenacted Affordable Housing Credit Improvement Act provisions, the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act and first-time buyer credits (Inman, October 29, 2026). Any bill still needs the President's signature, so bills with Republican cosponsors, such as the housing credit bill and Bennet's capital gains bill, stand the best chance. For Colorado projects: plan 2027 deals on current law (the larger ceiling and the 25% bond test) and not on bills that have not passed. Watch the December 11 funding deadline, Treasury's rules on large investors (the ban on new purchases by investors holding at least 350 homes generally starts January 7, 2027, per Inman), the calls in the 3rd and 4th Districts, and the Secretary of State's certification of congressional results by November 30, 2026.

briefs.title: New person-based measure estimates 53% of U.S. adults own their home
briefs.summary: The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis proposes the Homeowners-to-Population Ratio (HPOP), a person-based complement to the household-based owner-occupancy rate. Using American Community Survey microdata, HPOP classifies adult reference persons and their spouses or unmarried partners in owner-occupied homes as homeowners. For 2024, the researchers estimate that 53% of U.S. adults were homeowners, compared with an owner-occupancy rate of roughly 65%. HPOP sits about 12 points below the roughly 65% household-based owner-occupancy rate — the gap reflecting adults who live in owner-occupied homes without being the owner or their spouse/partner (e.g., adult children or other relatives). Among adults under 35, HPOP was about 22% — well below the roughly 37% owner-occupancy rate for households headed by someone under 35, which is a household-based measure and therefore not directly comparable. For Colorado, 2024 HPOP was 57.2% versus a 66.0% owner-occupancy rate — above the national HPOP. Because HPOP is published only at the state and metro (CBSA) levels, the available Colorado geographies are the state plus four metros: Fort Collins (HPOP 68.9%), Colorado Springs (68.5%), Denver-Aurora-Lakewood (63.2%), and Pueblo (41.5%). HPOP is not published for counties or places, so it cannot be reported for smaller Colorado jurisdictions such as Ignacio or Fruita. Source: Minneapolis Fed HPOP data, 2024.
briefs.implications: For COHO, HPOP should complement—not replace—the owner-occupancy rate. It can add person-level context to developer-oriented ownership analysis, including co-resident adults, delayed household formation, and disparities by age and demographic group. HPOP does not verify deed title for every adult, prove that co-resident adults will form separate households, or guarantee future rental demand. Local application should pair available state or metro HPOP estimates with household formation, cost burden, income, tenure, and supply data.

briefs.title: Colorado fee reductions for affordable housing: what towns waive, who pays, and how it differs by region
briefs.summary: COHO read the codes, fee schedules and council records of 48 Colorado jurisdictions and verified 118 local fee measures and 66 land-use or zoning incentives that lower the cost of affordable housing. Most fee relief is discretionary — 66 of 105 one-time fee measures need council or staff approval — and 96 of 118 fee measures do not say how the waived money is replaced. State law lets a local government waive an impact fee for low- or moderate-income or affordable employee housing (C.R.S. 29-20-104.5(5)) but does not require it, and a water or sewer utility run as an enterprise must keep grants from state and local governments under 10% of its annual revenue to stay outside TABOR. Consistent with that, utility fees are the ones cities repay from another fund: Loveland's Community Housing Development Fund repaid up to $366,070 of waived utility fees for Mirasol Phase III, while up to $504,807 of capital expansion fees on the same project were waived with no repayment, and Longmont may subsidize water and sewer system development fees only with money appropriated outside its utility funds. The regions differ. Mountain resort towns mostly waive fees outright for deed-restricted homes without an income cap — Mountain Village charges $21,650 per tap for a deed-restricted employee condo against $43,300 for a single-family home, and Telluride waives the in-town water and sewer tap attributable to a deed-restricted unit. Western Slope programs scale by income: Grand Junction waives 100% of city impact fees for rentals at or below 70% AMI, 75% at 71–80% AMI and 50% at 81–90% AMI, for a 30-year commitment. Front Range cities lean toward partial reductions, rebates after payment and income-qualified utility bill help: Colorado Springs rebates up to 100% of development charges after they are paid, Fort Collins credits up to $14,000 per unit, Littleton rebates $2,500 per affordable unit, Denver cuts the building permit fee $6,500 per income-restricted unit, and Westminster credits income-qualified households $360 a year on water bills. Deferrals (Fort Collins, Lafayette, Salida, Avon) are listed separately because a deferred fee is still owed. Screening context, not a study: what a jurisdiction offers is not what a project will receive.
briefs.implications: Four practical points. First, check who charges each fee: a town waiver may not reach a separate district — Aspen cannot waive school or sanitation district fees, and Grand Junction's program covers only city water and sewer, not Ute Water or Clifton Water. A special district has its own power to waive, amortize or defer its taps for affordable housing (C.R.S. 32-1-1001(1)(j)(II)), so the district is a separate ask. Second, count a waiver only once it is committed to the project; most are discretionary and several are subject to annual appropriation. Third, model a deferral as a loan with its trigger, not as a cost cut. Fourth, ask how a waiver is paid for: programs that name the paying fund (Grand Junction, Brighton, Loveland, Longmont) show where the money comes from; most do not. On land use, the 66 verified incentives in 39 jurisdictions are mostly inclusionary zoning with offsets, 90-day expedited review tied to the Proposition 123 fast-track, density bonuses and parking reductions. The Proposition 123 fast-track is a review deadline, not a fee rule. No Colorado statute found requires a local fee waiver for affordable housing; state bills since 2021 list fee waivers only as one optional strategy (HB21-1117, HB21-1271, HB24-1152, HB24-1313, SB24-174). Each jurisdiction's verified measures appear in its Housing Needs Assessment under local resources. The legal basis, how waived fees are paid for, the trends and numbered sources are in docs/methodology/LOCAL-JURISDICTION-HOUSING-CONTRIBUTIONS.md; the data is data/policy/fee-reductions.json.

briefs.title: HB26-1065 and Colorado’s Transit Zone credit: what the law establishes, what the adopted QAP sets, and what remains unknown
briefs.summary: Colorado HB26-1065 became law on May 27, 2026 and created Transit and Housing Investment Zones (THIZ), a state affordable-housing income-tax credit, and a separate sales-tax-increment mechanism for qualifying transit investment projects. The housing credit may be allocated by CHFA from 2027 through 2033, up to $8,333,333 annually, and is claimed over six credit years. Geographic eligibility depends on the official OEDIT THIZ map: the statute uses a two-mile zone around transportation facilities identified on that map. COHO’s tracked source was last checked November 3, 2026: OEDIT published the map that day, listing 10,980 existing and planned facilities, most of them bus stops. Program guidelines are not yet posted, and OEDIT says the map data is subject to change. A site check now uses OEDIT’s zone; transit-stop proximity is a screen, not an eligibility determination. CHFA’s 2027–2028 QAP, adopted by the CHFA Board on September 25, 2026 and approved by the Governor on October 23, 2026, calls the housing credit the Transit Zone (TZ) credit. The plan says it may be awarded under a separate TZ Credit Allocation Plan in lieu of standard state credit, not in addition to it. Under the adopted maximum-credit schedule, a 9% award may pair with a fixed $650,000 annual state or TZ credit in 2027 and $675,000 in 2028; a Round Two 4% award may pair with up to $675,000 annually in 2027 and $600,000 in 2028. Alternative amounts apply if the state gap-funding pilot is unavailable. These are annual credit amounts, not total project proceeds, and the separate TZ Credit Allocation Plan's terms are not final until adopted.
briefs.implications: The law, the OEDIT map and the QAP answer different questions. HB26-1065 creates the programs and statutory limits. OEDIT’s map determines whether an exact site is inside an eligible THIZ. CHFA’s QAP and separate allocation plan govern how an eligible rental project competes for and pairs the TZ credit. The adopted QAP’s ordinary TOD/TOC location criterion is separate: it gives five points for a qualifying site within a half-mile walk of transit, but those points do not themselves establish THIZ eligibility and are not TZ-credit-specific. The enacted bill and fiscal note do not create a distinct rural credit set-aside, bonus or enhanced rural amount; statewide geographic equity is a consideration for transit investment projects, not a substitute for zone eligibility. Until OEDIT publishes the authoritative map and CHFA adopts its TZ Credit Allocation Plan, a project should record the exact site, retain the screen as preliminary, show TZ funding as unavailable rather than zero, and avoid adding unawarded credit proceeds to a development budget. The Deal Calculator reads the same canonical legislation record and displays the applicable 9% or 4% pairing only after supported map eligibility; it does not silently add the amount to the capital stack.

briefs.title: The permanent 12% increase in the 9% LIHTC state ceiling: what the 2025 federal law changed
briefs.summary: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1), approved on July 4, 2025, changed how much housing credit each state may award every year. Section 70422(a) of the law amends section 42(h)(3)(I) of the Internal Revenue Code. Each state has an annual housing credit ceiling: the authority its housing credit agency uses to award credits outside the tax-exempt bond route, mainly the competitive credits commonly called 9% credits. Part of that ceiling is the greater of a per-resident amount or a small-state minimum. For calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025, the amended law multiplies both of those amounts by 1.12, a 12% increase, after the annual cost-of-living adjustment. The amended provision sets no end year. The same provision previously gave a 12.5% increase for 2018 through 2021 only. For 2026, IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 sets the amount at the greater of $3.416 per resident or $3,953,600, and lists the section 70422(a) amendment among the changes it reflects.
briefs.implications: The increase applies only to the per-resident or minimum amount. The other parts of a state's ceiling, which are unused credit carried forward from the prior year, credit returned during the year, and any national-pool allocation, are not multiplied. Section 70422(a) changes the size of each state's annual credit authority; it does not change the credit rate, the income and rent tests, or the eligible-basis rules for an individual building. The law's only other change to section 42 is the tax-exempt bond-financing test in section 70422(b), which COHO tracks as a separate record. In Colorado, CHFA allocates federal housing credits and administers the program under its Qualified Allocation Plan. Colorado's total for a year depends on the state population figure used and on any carried-forward or returned credit. COHO has not verified a 2026 Colorado total published by CHFA, so this brief does not state one. The legislation record lists January 1, 2026 as the effective date of the change.

briefs.title: The 25% bond-financing test for 4% LIHTC buildings: what the 2025 federal law changed
briefs.summary: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1), approved on July 4, 2025, changed the tax-exempt bond test that lets a building claim housing credits without an allocation from the state's annual credit ceiling. Buildings that qualify this way receive the credits commonly called 4% credits. Section 70422(b) of the law rewrites section 42(h)(4)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code. Before the change, the test had one route: tax-exempt private activity bonds counted against the state's volume cap had to finance 50% or more of the aggregate basis of the building and the land under it. The amended provision keeps that 50% route and adds a second one. A building also qualifies if such bonds finance 25% or more of that basis, as long as one or more of those bonds come from an issue dated after December 31, 2025 and together finance at least 5% of the basis. The change applies to buildings placed in service in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. The amended provision sets no end year.
briefs.implications: A building can now meet the test with a smaller share of bond financing than before, so the same amount of volume cap can support credits for more buildings. Bonds issued before 2026 still count toward the 25%, but only when bonds from post-2025 issues together provide at least 5% of the basis; that 5% can come from more than one such bond. For a rehabilitation that is treated as a separate new building, section 70422(b)(2)(B) treats both the existing building and the rehabilitation as placed in service on the date the rehabilitation expenditures are. The change does not alter the credit rate, the income and rent tests, or the state's annual credit ceiling. The law's other change to section 42, the 12% ceiling increase in section 70422(a), has its own COHO brief. In Colorado, the Department of Local Affairs receives the state's volume cap; CHFA's December 4, 2025 stakeholder presentation says that by statute 50% goes to statewide authorities, including CHFA, and 50% to local governments. In the same presentation CHFA said new CHFA multifamily lending and 2026 Round Two projects would use not more than 45% bond financing, lower when feasible. COHO has not verified a CHFA policy for later years, so this brief does not state one.

briefs.title: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: what the 2026 federal housing law changes for affordable rental financing
briefs.summary: H.R. 6644, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, became law on July 11, 2026 as Public Law 119-101. A note by the Office of the Federal Register on the law says it was presented to the President on June 29, 2026 and became law without his signature because it was not returned within the time the Constitution allows. The House gave its final approval on June 23, 2026. The law reforms federal housing-supply and HUD programs. It does not amend section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code, so it does not change housing tax credit ceilings, credit rates or eligibility rules. Section 1202 says no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the law or its amendments.
briefs.implications: The provisions below bear most directly on financing affordable rental housing. Section 204 makes the new construction of affordable housing an eligible Community Development Block Grant activity, limited to 20% of the amounts allocated to the recipient, and only for amounts appropriated after the date of enactment. Section 501 changes the HOME Investment Partnerships program: section 501(i) repeals the rule under which a participating jurisdiction lost the right to draw HOME funds it had not committed within 24 months, and section 501(l) exempts four categories of HOME activity from review under the National Environmental Policy Act: new construction infill housing projects, acquisition of real property for affordable housing, certain rehabilitation projects, and new construction projects of 15 units or less. An infill housing project must, among other tests, sit on previously disturbed land of not more than 5 acres. HUD must issue any rules it determines necessary for the exemptions within 1 year of enactment. Section 405(a) lets a voucher unit in a housing tax credit building meet the Housing Choice Voucher inspection requirement if it was physically inspected and met the suitability-for-occupancy requirement in section 42(i)(3)(B)(ii) during the preceding 12 months, and the public housing agency performed that inspection itself or can obtain its results. COHO searched the Federal Register on October 11, 2026 and found no HUD rule or notice putting the section 204 or section 501 changes into effect, so this brief does not describe how HUD will apply them. COHO has not verified any Colorado grantee's plan to use the new CDBG activity.

briefs.title: Colorado's local-government right of first refusal and right of first offer (HB24-1175): what it requires through 2029
briefs.summary: Colorado House Bill 24-1175, approved by the Governor on May 30, 2024 and effective August 7, 2024, gives local governments two rights to buy certain multifamily rental properties. It adds sections 29-4-1201 to 29-4-1208 to the Colorado Revised Statutes. Under section 29-4-1202, the city, town or county where the property is located has a right of first refusal, exercised with a matched offer, on a rental property of 5 units or more that is existing affordable housing, meaning it is subject to a recorded restricted-use covenant or similar affordability agreement. Under section 29-4-1203, it has a right of first offer on other rental properties of at least 15 units and not more than 100 units, which the seller must notify it about before engaging a licensed broker to find buyers or listing the property on the multiple listing service. Either right may be used only to keep or convert the property as long-term affordable housing, which the act defines to include affordability for at least 40 years; the right of first offer also allows a mixed-income development. Under section 29-4-1207 both rights terminate on December 31, 2029, except that a process the local government began before that date continues until it concludes. Section 29-4-1208 repeals the part on July 1, 2031.
briefs.implications: For a covenant-restricted property, including one financed with housing tax credits, the seller must notify CHFA and the local government at least 2 years, and again at least 6 months, before the last affordability restriction expires. When a sale is in prospect, the seller must notify the local government within 14 calendar days of a triggering event, such as signing a letter of intent, listing the property, or conditionally accepting an offer. The local government is to tell the seller within 14 calendar days of receiving that notice whether it intends to preserve or waive its right of first refusal, and then has 30 calendar days to make an offer, and must agree to close within 60 calendar days after the seller accepts, or within the period in a third-party buyer's all-cash offer if the seller has one. If the price in the seller's notice drops by 5% or more, or its terms or conditions materially change, the seller must give notice within 7 days and the local government may exercise or re-exercise the right. The local government and the seller may extend any of these periods by written agreement. The right of first offer does not apply if the property's first certificate of occupancy was issued within the 30 years before the listing. Section 29-4-1205 exempts several kinds of transfer, including a sale by a seller that has applied for, is in the process of, or has completed a resyndication or recapitalization under a public affordable housing program, if the seller gives the local government notice and evidence of it; the rights apply again if that effort fails. A local government may assign either right to a local or regional housing authority or to CHFA. Under section 29-4-1206 the remedies are damages and statutory penalties against the seller: a court must award at least $10,000 for a first material violation and at least $30,000 for a later one, and no more than $100,000, and a buyer taking title through the seller takes it free of these rights. COHO has not verified which Colorado local governments have waived or assigned their rights, so this brief does not list them.
