briefs.title: Designing affordable rental housing people can live in: accessibility, supportive housing and shared space
briefs.takeaway: Colorado law already sets how many accessible homes a publicly funded building, or a privately funded one of seven or more homes, must have, and CHFA's adopted 2027-28 plan adds two points for universal design or Type A units in at least 5% of homes. Settle accessibility, room sizes, laundry and the shared rooms on the first site plan. Changing them after the drawings are done costs far more, and no study supports putting a dollar value on them in a pro forma.
briefs.summary: Colorado sets its own accessibility floor. The law covers housing built with public money and privately funded buildings of seven or more homes (C.R.S. 9-5-103). Under its point schedule (C.R.S. 9-5-105), a project needs 6 accessibility points for 7 to 14 homes and 6 more for every further 14 homes or part of 14. A Type A home counts 6 points and a Type B home 4, so a 60-home building needs 30 points, for example five Type A homes. Since SB26-109 (signed May 5, 2026), a project of 50 or more homes must also make at least 2% of its homes accessible units; smaller projects may use any mix. Projects with HUD money also carry Section 504: 5% of homes for people with mobility impairments and another 2% for people with hearing or vision impairments. The State Demography Office's forecast has Coloradans aged 65 and older growing from about 870,000 in 2020 to about 1.14 million in 2030, 18.2% of residents. A building financed today will house many of them over its compliance period and the years after it. The best-tested part of this brief is supportive housing itself: in Denver's randomized trial, 77% of the people it housed, not counting those who died, were still housed three years later. Design for supportive housing is much less tested. Trauma-informed design came out of Denver work by Shopworks Architecture and the University of Denver, and the one comparison study so far, at five sites, found mixed results. Evidence on green space is stronger than evidence on building layout. A randomized trial in Philadelphia found that greening vacant lots cut shootings and that nearby residents reported feeling depressed less often. Evidence on shared rooms, porches and privacy comes mostly from surveys and interviews. CHFA's 2027-28 QAP, adopted on September 25, 2026 and approved by the Governor on October 23, 2026, requires green building certification, water-wise landscaping and the same unit design for every income tier, and awards two points for universal design or accessible Type A units in at least 5% of units.
briefs.implications: Count the accessibility points on the first site plan. The mix of Type A and Type B homes, the step-free route from parking and the bus stop to each entrance, door widths and grab-bar blocking are cheap at schematic design and expensive after construction drawings. If the project is going after CHFA's two universal design points, decide at the same time whether Type A homes will be at least 5% of the total. Use CHFA's rules as the design brief: the same finishes and square footage at every income tier, affordable homes spread through each building, no locked laundry closets, green building certification and no non-functional turf. Plant shade trees and water-wise beds where residents will sit, and put the community room on the way to the mailboxes and laundry. For supportive housing, decide before the floor plans where residents first meet staff, how they control who comes to their door, and how people who have been homeless will review the plans. Sanderson Apartments in Denver, 60 homes opened in 2017, put its community, dining and exercise rooms by the front desk and used open cabinets and wide, windowed corridors so residents can see who is around. Leave design out of the deal model's numbers, because no study gives a dollar figure for it. Use this brief for design priorities and the QAP narrative, and the Deal Calculator for costs and financing.

sections.heading: Universal access: homes anyone can use without help
paragraphs: Universal design means designing a place so that as many people as possible can use it without adaptation and without being singled out. The seven principles written at North Carolina State University's Center for Universal Design in 1997 are still the clearest test: equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use. Four of the seven are about usability, not access codes, so a space can pass an accessibility inspection and still be hard to use.

Colorado's accessibility law covers buildings built with public money and privately funded buildings of seven or more homes (C.R.S. 9-5-103). Each project needs accessibility points by unit count (C.R.S. 9-5-105): 6 points for 7 to 14 homes, 12 for 15 to 28, and 6 more for every further 14 homes or part of 14. A Type A home counts 6 points, a Type A multistory home 5, a Type B home 4, a Type B multistory home 3 and a Type C visitable home 1. SB26-109, signed May 5, 2026 and effective immediately, renamed the one-point type (formerly Type B visitable ground floor) and limited the free mix to projects under 50 homes: at 50 or more, at least 2% of homes must be accessible units, including at least one Type A, Type B or Type C home. The legislature declared the standards a matter of statewide concern, and local governments may adopt stricter ones (C.R.S. 9-5-103).

Federal rules add to that. The Fair Housing Act requires seven accessibility features in covered multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991: in every unit of an elevator building, and in ground-floor units otherwise. Projects with HUD funds, such as HOME, must also meet Section 504: at least 5% of units accessible for people with mobility impairments and another 2% for people with hearing or vision impairments. CHFA's adopted 2027-28 QAP adds two points for universal design or for Type A accessible units in at least 5% of units. Zero-step entrances and wider doors cost little when planned into new construction and are much harder to add later (Maisel, Smith and Steinfeld, 2008).

The need in Colorado is growing. The State Demography Office's single-year-of-age forecast has residents aged 65 and older rising from about 870,000 in 2020 (15.0% of residents) to about 1.14 million in 2030 (18.2%) and about 1.49 million in 2050 (20.7%). A rental building financed now will house many households over its compliance period and after it.

The next two sections cover residents for whom a step-free route is not enough: neuro-inclusive design for people who process noise and light differently, and trauma-informed design for people who have been homeless.
sections.items_heading: What highly usable looks like in practice
items: One step-free route from the sidewalk, parking, drop-off and bus stop to every entrance, and on to the mailroom, laundry, trash room, community room and outdoor space.
Covered, well-lit entrances with a power-operated or easy-to-open door, a shelf to set things down and a bench nearby.
Wayfinding that works without signs: daylight at the ends of corridors, a different color or material at each floor and door, no dead-end corridors, and signs readable from a seated height.
Lever handles, rocker switches, thermostats and outlets within reach, front-control ranges, and clear floor space at the sink and the bed.
Curbless or low-threshold showers, wall blocking for grab bars in every home, and room to turn a wheelchair.
sections.note: These practices follow the seven principles, Colorado's accessibility law and the Fair Housing Act. They were not each tested in a trial.

sections.heading: Neuro-inclusive design: calm spaces that make sense
paragraphs: Neuro-inclusive design plans for how people take in their surroundings: noise, light, smell, crowding and how easy a place is to understand. It matters most for residents who are autistic or have ADHD, dementia or another neurological difference. The UK's PAS 6463:2022, Design for the mind, was the first national guidance on it. It covers homes for independent or supported living as well as public buildings, and addresses lighting, acoustics, décor, flooring, layout, wayfinding, familiarity, thermal comfort and smell. It is guidance, not a code.

Magda Mostafa's ASPECTSS Design Index, published in 2014, names seven criteria: acoustics, spatial sequencing, escape spaces, compartmentalization, transitions, sensory zoning and safety. For housing, Arizona State University's Advancing Full Spectrum Housing (2010), by Sherry Ahrentzen and Kim Steele and a companion to ULI Arizona's Opening Doors, set ten resident-based design goals for adults with autism, running from neighborhood amenities to assistive technology in the home.

The evidence for housing is thin. The studies behind ASPECTSS are post-occupancy evaluations of schools, built on staff surveys and classroom observation, and this review found no study that measured resident outcomes in affordable rental housing. Most of these choices cost little if they are made before the floor plans.
sections.items_heading: What it looks like in a building
items: Laundry, trash rooms, elevators and mechanical equipment kept away from bedroom walls, busy shared rooms kept apart from quiet ones, and sound separation between homes and corridors better than the code minimum.
Even, glare-free lighting that residents can dim, with daylight and no flickering or buzzing fixtures, and colors and signs used the same way on every floor.
One obvious route from entry to mail to elevator to home, with a place to pause at the building entry and at each front door.
A small quiet room or alcove off a busy shared space, where someone can step away without leaving.

see_also.text: For how this housing is financed, staffed and filled in Colorado, see the neuro-inclusive housing brief.

sections.heading: Permanent supportive housing: design for safety, choice and recovery
paragraphs: Permanent supportive housing pairs a standard lease with services residents choose to use, for people leaving long-term homelessness who live with a disability. Most follows Housing First, which does not require sobriety or treatment to get or keep the home. The model is well tested. In Denver's Supportive Housing Social Impact Bond, a randomized trial of 724 people, 77% of those it housed, not counting those who died, were still in stable housing three years later, and the supportive housing group had 40% fewer arrests and 27% fewer days in jail than people who received usual services (Urban Institute, 2021). In Canada's At Home/Chez Soi trial in five cities, 62% of Housing First participants were housed all of the time in the study's last six months, against 31% of those who received usual services.

Design for supportive housing is newer and less proven. The most developed approach comes from Colorado: trauma-informed design, built by Shopworks Architecture, Group14 Engineering and the University of Denver's Center for Housing and Homelessness Research, with research funders that include CHFA. It puts safety, real and perceived, first, followed by comfort, choice and connection, and its authors say it is not a checklist. A 2022 scoping review of 13 studies found that the evidence lines up with these principles but is limited, mostly qualitative and from few places (Owen and Crane). The first quasi-experimental test, at five supportive housing sites, three designed this way and two not, found mixed results: some measures of relationships improved at the trauma-informed sites, while measures of psychological safety fell and reported conflict rose over the study. The authors conclude that safety, conflict and relationships change together as residents settle in (Brisson and colleagues, 2025).

Two Denver buildings show what this looks like. Sanderson Apartments, 60 furnished homes of about 440 square feet for people who had been chronically homeless, opened in 2017 and is run by the Mental Health Center of Denver. Its community, dining and exercise rooms sit by the front desk, corridors are wider and lined with windows, and kitchen cabinets and closets have no doors, so residents can see what is there and who is around. Arroyo Village, designed by Shopworks and opened in March 2019, combines a shelter, supportive housing and workforce housing, with no intake desk, lockers, and privacy walls between shelter beds. Neither has been studied; the descriptions come from news reports.

CHFA asks for this design. Points for homelessness and special-population set-asides under QAP 5.B.5 require design suited to the population served, such as trauma-informed design, services residents can choose at no cost, and tenant selection that follows Housing First practices such as pet-friendly policies. The adopted 2027-28 plan also bars locked laundry closets as a minimum amenity, unless CHFA allows an exception in its sole discretion.
sections.items_heading: Questions to settle before the floor plans
items: Where does a resident first meet staff, and does the entry feel welcoming rather than guarded?
Can people see who is in a shared room before they go in, and leave it another way?
Is there a private room for meeting a case manager or a nurse that is not on a corridor everyone uses?
Can each resident control their own light, heat, noise and who comes to the door?
Where do pets go, and where can residents store belongings securely?
Are there places to be near other people without having to talk, such as a porch, a window seat or a bench by the entry?
How did people with lived experience of homelessness shape the design, and how will the team learn from residents after move-in?

sections.heading: Design for community: public and private spaces that work together
paragraphs: People meet their neighbors in the spaces between the street and the front door, so those spaces need a clear order. Christopher Alexander's A Pattern Language (1977) calls it an intimacy gradient: arrange a building so a person moves from the most public places, through shared ones, to the most private. When each step is clear, residents can choose how much contact they want. Jan Gehl's studies of residential streets found that soft edges, such as front yards, porches and stoops where people can sit and putter, give residents of all ages reasons to stay outside, and make the street livelier for it.

Shared space helps residents get to know neighbors, and that reduces loneliness, but most of the evidence is interviews and surveys rather than trials. Social-housing tenants in New Zealand, most of them over 55 and living alone, described common areas as where neighbor ties began and grew into mutual help. A survey of multifamily residents found that those with more shared amenities knew more neighbors and felt less lonely, and that everyday spaces such as lobbies and laundry rooms mattered as much as courtyards.

A community room on the way to the mailboxes gets used; one behind a locked door at the end of a corridor does not. Resident services are part of the same picture: industry studies of properties with on-site services report lower rent arrears and fewer eviction move-outs, though none of them is a controlled study.

Some of these spaces can serve the neighborhood as well as residents: a ground-floor clinic, child care center, café or public courtyard. They turn the building's edge toward the street, but they need a clear line where public use ends and residents' space begins, such as a separate entrance or a gate residents control. In supportive housing that line matters more, because control over who comes in is part of safety.

steps.caption: From street to home: each step a little more private

items.label: Street
items.text: Sidewalk, street trees, lighting and windows that look out on it.

items.label: Front edge
items.text: A porch, stoop, front garden or bench where residents can sit and see the street, and any ground-floor use the neighborhood shares.

items.label: Shared rooms
items.text: Lobby, mail, laundry, courtyard and community room, on the routes residents already walk.

items.label: Near the door
items.text: A short corridor or shared landing serving a handful of homes, with a spot to pause.

items.label: Home
items.text: A real entry, a door that closes, and rooms the household controls.

sections.heading: Smaller homes and porches
paragraphs: Affordable homes are often smaller than market-rate ones, and CHFA's QAP sets no minimum unit size by bedroom count. Layout can make a small home work. In a study of 9-year-olds, Evans and Rollings found that higher bedroom ceilings weakened the link between feeling crowded at home and physiological stress. For older residents, one-floor living matters most: in a national sample of 7,197 adults aged 65 and older, having the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom on one floor was among the home features most strongly linked to staying in place rather than moving (Granbom et al., 2018). Drawing each plan with the furniture the household will own catches rooms that are too small before they are built.

Jan Gehl's studies of residential streets in Australia, Canada and Scandinavia found more lingering and street life where front yards, forecourts and porches form a 'soft edge' between home and street. In 10 Portland neighborhoods, Wilkerson and colleagues found more neighborliness where front porches and continuous sidewalks give people semi-private space for casual contact, though several of their results were not statistically significant. A porch only does this if two people can sit on it.
sections.items_heading: What makes a small home and its porch functional
items: Storage where it is used: an entry closet, a pantry, linen storage and bedroom closets, drawn on the plan rather than left to leftover corners.
A defined entry with room to stop, drop keys and bags, and take off boots, so the living room is not also the hallway.
A kitchen counter that doubles as a table when there is no room for a dining area.
Rooms checked against the furniture the household will own: beds, a dresser, a desk or homework table, and a table that seats everyone.
Daylight and a view from the main living space, from two sides where the plan allows, and taller ceilings where the budget allows.
For older residents and anyone with limited mobility: the kitchen, a bedroom and a full bathroom on the entry level, with a step-free route from parking to the door.

A covered, lit porch at least 5 feet deep facing the shared walk rather than the parking lot, with room for two chairs and a screen between neighbors, plus a private patio or yard at the back where the site allows.

sections.heading: Green infrastructure, health and happiness
paragraphs: This is the strongest body of evidence in the brief, and it includes randomized trials.

In Colorado, green infrastructure should mean shade trees, native and water-wise planting, and outdoor rooms people use, not lawn. CHFA now limits non-functional turf. Shade matters here too: across 108 U.S. urban areas, formerly redlined neighborhoods are hotter at ground level than their neighbors, by as much as 7°C (about 12°F), and Denver had one of the largest gaps.

table.caption: What the studies found
rows: People in Philadelphia living near vacant lots that were greened reported feeling depressed and worthless less often; neighbors of untreated lots did not (South et al., 2018).
Greening vacant lots reduced shootings by 6.8% in the same Philadelphia trial (Branas et al., 2018).

The same people reported higher life satisfaction and less mental distress in the years they lived in greener urban areas. The effect was about a third of the life-satisfaction gain associated with marriage (White et al., 2013).
UK panel, 1991-2008, comparing the same people over time
Across more than a million smartphone mood reports, people were happier outdoors in natural settings than in built-up ones (MacKerron and Mourato, 2013).
People who spent at least 120 minutes a week in nature were more likely to report high well-being and good health; under 120 minutes showed no benefit (White et al., 2019).
Danish children with the least green space near home had up to 55% higher risk of later psychiatric disorders than those with the most (Engemann et al., 2019).
Chicago public housing residents assigned to buildings with more trees and grass outside reported less aggression and violence (Kuo and Sullivan, 2001).

One year after a green rehab to Enterprise Green Communities standards, adults in a 60-unit Minnesota property reported better general health and less asthma, bronchitis and sinusitis (Breysse et al., 2011).
Before and after, no control group
Children with asthma in green public housing in Boston had fewer symptoms, attacks and asthma-related school absences than children in conventional units (Colton et al., 2015).

sections.heading: Privacy, crowding and quiet
paragraphs: Crowding is linked to worse wellbeing in children, with more distress, more conflict with parents and more learned helplessness, regardless of household income, and Gary Evans's research found the effects were stronger in large multifamily buildings. The design response is bedroom counts that fit the households the market study expects, a door that closes on a place to study, and enough storage that a living room does not become a storeroom.

The WHO's 2018 noise guidelines link traffic noise to disturbed sleep and cardiovascular disease, which matters for sites next to highways and rail lines. Evidence on noise from neighbors is thinner, but complaints about it are common. Separate homes acoustically, and keep mechanical equipment, trash rooms and elevators away from bedroom walls.

sections.heading: Safety and dignity
paragraphs: Oscar Newman's defensible-space argument held that building form drove crime in public housing. A federal review found that only limited reliable conclusions could be drawn from his studies, and his central comparison did not account for the different share of children in the two projects. Clear sightlines, entrances that face the street and good lighting are still sensible, but the evidence does not show they are enough on their own.

Dignity has a direct rule in Colorado. CHFA’s QAP requires every income tier to get units with the same amenities and square footage, asks the same of market-rate units to the extent possible, and spreads affordable units through each building and, where it can, each floor. A separate wing of smaller or plainer affordable units works against that rule.

sections.heading: Limits of this brief
paragraphs: Most studies here are observational, small, or both, and several come from one research group. Only the Philadelphia greening trial and the Denver and Canadian supportive housing trials are randomized, and the housing trials test the model of a lease plus services, not the design of the building. Neuro-inclusive and trauma-informed design rest mostly on expert guidance, interviews and studies of schools or a few sites, and the two Denver buildings are described from news reports, not studies. None of the studies measured effects on operating costs in Colorado affordable housing, so the brief gives no dollar figures, and none should be added to a deal model on its strength. The QAP items come from the adopted 2027-28 plan. COHO checks each quoted requirement against the machine-extracted text of the named CHFA document on every build, but the PDF is the authority.

briefs.title: Neuro-inclusive housing in Colorado: how it gets built, paid for and filled
briefs.takeaway: Housing for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) works best as ordinary affordable homes with a share set aside and services paid separately by Medicaid. The building is the easier part. The hard part is the money for services, and Colorado is slowing new enrollments in its main disability waiver.
briefs.summary: CHFA calls this housing neuro-inclusive: designed for people with I/DD but open to everyone. In Colorado it is built in a few ways: a set-aside of homes in a tax-credit building, a group home, a community with staff on site around the clock, or a home a family buys. In every model the rent and the services are paid from different pots. Medicaid waivers pay for support but not for rent, and in provider-run homes the state caps what a resident can be charged for room and board at $810 a month in 2026. CHFA's adopted 2027-28 plan gives fifteen points for setting aside at least 25 percent of homes for Special Populations, which include people with developmental and intellectual impairments.
briefs.implications: Line up the service provider before the site. CHFA wants signed agreements with providers that have at least three years of experience, a services budget and a source of residents. Keep the I/DD homes to about a quarter of the building and spread them through it: in a building with federal Section 811 rental assistance, no more than 25% of homes may be set aside for, or give preference to, people with disabilities, and Medicaid treats a setting that isolates people as institutional. Plan for transport, because most adults with I/DD do not drive. Use the developer-fee increase CHFA allows for Special Populations to fund services, because no Colorado program pays for a building-wide support desk.

sections.heading: What the words mean
paragraphs: Intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) begin in childhood and limit learning, everyday living skills or both. Colorado's definition (C.R.S. 25.5-10-202) names cerebral palsy, epilepsy, autism and Prader-Willi syndrome among the related conditions. A diagnosis of I/DD is what opens the door to Colorado's disability waivers, which pay for support at home.

Neurodivergent describes a person. Neuro-inclusive describes housing. In CHFA's words, neuro-inclusive housing "considers the physical and cognitive accessibility needs of individuals with I/DD, but is not exclusively for this population."

see_also.text: For calm, easy-to-read building design, see the neuro-inclusive design section of the livability brief.

sections.heading: How many Coloradans need it
items: At least 127,000 Coloradans with I/DD have asked for services, and 73% live with aging family caregivers (CHFA white paper, 2022).
At least 20,000 live with a caregiver over 60. When that parent dies or falls ill, the adult child often has nowhere planned to go.
2,749 people were waiting "as soon as available" for the comprehensive (DD) waiver, the one that pays for support around the clock, as of September 2025 (Joint Budget Committee staff, March 2026).
Most rely on Supplemental Security Income, which pays at most $994 a month in 2026, so rent has to be deeply subsidized.

sections.heading: Five ways it gets built in Colorado
paragraphs: Every model answers two questions: who pays the rent, and who pays for support. CHFA's white paper urges separating the two, so a resident can change service provider without losing their home. CHFA calls that a consumer-controlled setting.

sections.heading: The Mirasol model: small homes with care around the clock
paragraphs: The Green House Homes at Mirasol in Loveland are six homes for elders, each for 10-12 residents, licensed together as one skilled nursing facility. They opened in 2014, built by the Loveland Housing Authority with a nursing-home operator. The financing stack: a total project cost of $16,784,326, $10,340,000 of New Markets Tax Credit allocation, $2.6 million from the Colorado Division of Housing, $584,000 in fee waivers from the city of Loveland and a $2 million foundation grant.

It works because a nursing home is paid one Medicaid daily rate that covers care, the room and the food. Federal rules let Medicaid pay for room and board in institutions but not in community settings, where a waiver may not pay for room and board. So a Mirasol-style building is funded once, through the care rate.

For adults with I/DD, the matching license is an intermediate care facility (ICF/IID), which federal rules count as an institution, not a home and community-based setting. Colorado's waivers instead pay for support while the resident pays rent. The comprehensive waiver "provides access to 24-hour, seven days a week supervision", but the resident still pays room and board from Supplemental Security Income, capped at $810 a month.
sections.items_heading: What carries over to I/DD housing
items: Small homes with private rooms and the same few staff every day. This is the design lesson, and it works with any license.
Pay for the building with grants and tax credits, not debt. Capped rent cannot carry a mortgage.
Keep the landlord and the care provider separate, so residents keep their home if they change provider.
Do not cluster homes in a way that cuts residents off from neighbors. Medicaid presumes such a setting is institutional unless it passes a federal review.
sections.note: COHO arithmetic, not from a source: one post staffed around the clock is 8,760 hours a year, about 4.2 full-time staff. A six-person group home collects at most $4,860 a month in room and board at the 2026 cap, for rent, utilities, food and upkeep together.

sections.heading: The real gap: money for support
items: Colorado is slowing new enrollments. The governor's January 2026 budget request proposed "reducing by half the number of individuals automatically enrolled from the waitlist" for the DD waiver, and ending automatic enrollment of young people who age out of children's services. A news report says the Joint Budget Committee approved a rule of one new enrollment for every two people who leave (news report, not yet checked against the final budget bill).
Group-home rent is capped. Providers may charge at most $810 a month for room and board in 2026, and residents keep a personal needs allowance of at least $184.

Residential rates are being reset. The same budget request proposed "a lower rate for settings with a primary live in caregiver" and "a higher rate for settings with rotating staff". It noted these rates had risen about 36% over five years.
Case management changed in 2024. Agencies had to be conflict-free by July 1, 2024, and the redesign aims to put case management for every waiver in one place.
Transport is thin. RTD declined to extend Access-a-Ride paratransit to Grove at Cottonwood (news report, March 2026).

sections.heading: What CHFA scores
items: Fifteen points for setting aside at least 25% of homes for Special Populations. CHFA may accept a smaller share where a federal or state rule limits the number of special needs homes, such as Section 811.

To earn the points: a services plan, a services budget showing enough staff, signed agreements with providers that have at least three years of experience, evidence of where residents will come from, and design suited to the people served.

The developer fee can rise by up to 5%, pro-rated by the share of homes for Special Populations at or below 30% of area income, and only if at least 15% of all homes are at or below 30% of area income. The extra fee must pay for services or rent help.
These rules come from CHFA's adopted 2027-28 plan.

sections.heading: Filling the homes
items: Grove at Cottonwood, Broomfield, held its grand opening in September 2026. Denver7 reported 10 residents moved in, 10 more preparing to move in and 20 homes still available.

In Indiana, a quarter of the homes at SouthPointe Village in Fishers were set aside for residents with disabilities. Pre-leased homes were full before the grand opening, with a call list of more than 400 people (2021).
Diamond View in South Bend, Indiana, has 60 homes, including 12 three-bedroom homes set aside for adults with I/DD, and space in the building for The Logan Center, a local disability agency (2024).

Indiana's 2024 award entry reports that its then-current plan set aside 10% of its tax credits for developments serving people with I/DD and brain injuries, and that in the six years since 2018 the set-aside produced 362 homes in 32 developments. Colorado has no such set-aside.

sections.heading: Vouchers, preferences and fair housing
paragraphs: In short: you cannot turn away a voucher holder. You can favor people with disabilities, or people who qualify for the services you offer. You cannot favor one diagnosis.
items: Colorado law (C.R.S. 24-34-502) has barred refusing to rent because of source of income since January 2021, including government rental assistance. Very small landlords are exempt.
A tax-credit building's recorded agreement must forbid refusing a voucher holder because they hold a voucher (26 U.S.C. 42(h)(6)(B)(iv)).
A set-aside is still allowed. Federal tax law says a tax-credit project keeps its general public use status when it favors tenants with special needs (26 U.S.C. 42(g)(9)).

With project-based vouchers, the owner may prefer people who qualify for voluntary services offered at the building, including disability-specific services. The owner may advertise services for a particular disability, but may not limit the preference to a specific disability, and services must stay voluntary (24 CFR 983.251(d)).

In a building with Section 811 rental assistance, no more than 25% of homes may be set aside for people with disabilities or carry a disability preference, counting other programs too. The homes must be spread through the building, and people with disabilities may still apply for every other home.

Vouchers in group homes: federal rules allow a voucher in a state-approved group home of up to 12 residents. But a housing authority is not required to permit this unless a resident needs it as a reasonable accommodation (24 CFR 982.601 and 982.610).

sections.heading: Who builds and supports this housing in Colorado
items: State agencies: CHFA (research, financing and the tax-credit plan); the Division of Housing (Section 811, state vouchers and supportive housing funding); the Department of Health Care Policy and Financing (disability waivers and case management agencies).

Advocacy and research: Inclusive Housing Coalition; Root Policy Research, CHFA's research partner on 2026 statewide neuro-inclusive open houses; Neuro-Inclusive Housing Solutions, which wrote CHFA's white paper; Alliance, the association of community centered boards and providers; Parent to Parent of Colorado.

Builders and owners: Broomfield Housing Alliance with BlueLine Development (Grove at Cottonwood); RealAmerica with Community Options (Cedar Creek Commons); Boulder Housing Partners (30PRL); Wellspring Community; Trailhead Community; Tall Tales Ranch; Loveland Housing Authority (Mirasol).

Service and support partners named at the 2024 Neuro-Inclusive Housing Summit: Imagine!, Bayaud Enterprises (housing navigation), Firefly Autism, Blue Star Recyclers (jobs), Ascendigo (Yellow House) and Shopworks Architecture (design).

items: The need figures come from CHFA's 2022 white paper and are not updated each year.
Lease-up figures are from news reports, not owner records.

briefs.title: Shared equity in Colorado: how for-sale and rental housing can build household wealth and stay affordable
briefs.takeaway: Shared equity trades some of a household's upside for a home that stays affordable to the next household. The evidence that it keeps homes affordable and keeps owners in them is good; the evidence on how much wealth it builds is thinner, and on the rental side most models are new. Pick the resale or equity rule first, because it decides who the project serves in year 20, not just at opening.
briefs.summary: Shared equity is any arrangement in which a public or nonprofit investment makes a home affordable and a rule written into the deed, ground lease, co-op shares or partnership agreement keeps it affordable afterwards, while the household still keeps part of the gain. Grounded Solutions Network describes it as a model that takes a one-time public investment and then restricts the home's sale price each time it is sold. On the for-sale side the established forms are community land trust ground leases, deed-restricted homes with a resale formula, and limited-equity cooperatives. A shared-appreciation loan is related but different: the home resells at market price and the lender, not the next buyer, gets the share of the gain. On the rental side the forms are newer: resident-owned manufactured home communities, renter equity programs that pay tenants a share of savings, LIHTC buildings sold to tenants or a nonprofit after the 15-year compliance period, and in Colorado the tenant equity vehicle that state law requires in projects funded by the Proposition 123 equity program. Studies of established for-sale programs find that resold homes stayed affordable and that foreclosure was rare; a 2019 study of 4,108 shared equity homes found the median household accumulated approximately $14,000 against a median equity investment at purchase of $1,875. The trade-off is real: the same studies find that a formula giving sellers more return makes the home less affordable to the next buyer.
briefs.implications: For a for-sale project, settle the steward and the resale rule before the pro forma, because the rule decides the price the second and third buyers pay and what the first owner walks away with. The For-Sale Market Study runs the same appreciation scenarios through each resale convention side by side and does not rank them, because they optimize different things. Mountain towns already buy deed restrictions on existing homes; that is a way to add shared-equity homes without building, and the table below lists the programs this site has on record. For a rental project funded by the Proposition 123 equity program, the tenant equity vehicle is not optional: tenants who stay at least a year are entitled by statute to a share of any equity growth. The program pays that share from its own returns above its initial investment, so confirm with the program's administrator how the vehicle runs in the project and what it asks of the owner. For a manufactured home community, state law gives residents notice and a time-limited opportunity to buy the park, and Proposition 123 can fund the purchase. Budget for stewardship in every model. A resale rule that nobody monitors is a rule that lapses, and the study of land trust loan performance found that only a minority of land trusts had outside funding to expand or support their work.

The Market Study models the three percent part and not the improvement credits; a unit's own deed restriction can set a different formula, so read it before relying on the rate. Breckenridge's Housing Helps program, created by Resolution 17 (Series 2019), pays owners, buyers and local businesses 15-25% for a deed restriction on unrestricted homes: 15% for a light work-requirement restriction, 20-25% for a full restriction with a 3% appreciation cap.

sections.heading: Rental and resident-ownership models
paragraphs: Shared equity for renters is newer and has far less evidence behind it. The models below either let residents buy the property together, or pay tenants a share of what their tenancy saves or earns the owner.
items: Resident-owned manufactured home communities. Residents form a cooperative and buy the land under their homes. ROC USA reports, from a longitudinal study by an appraisal firm, that site fees in its member communities were 11% below market after five years and 21% below market after 10 years. ROC USA documented the Meadowood Village residents' purchase of their park in Littleton in January 2025.

Renter equity. Cornerstone Corporation for Shared Equity's model in Cincinnati, used by Northeast Shores in Cleveland, gives tenants credits for paying rent on time, following house rules and doing work on the property, paid from savings on turnover and vacancy. Next City reported in 2015 that renters could earn up to $10,000 over 10 years. No independent evaluation was found.

Proposition 123 tenant equity vehicle. State law requires the equity program to include a tenant equity vehicle: in projects it funds, tenants who live there at least one year are entitled to a share of the equity growth, if any, as funding for a down payment or related purposes, which may also include ongoing opportunities to build up savings. Program returns above the initial investment stay in the program to fund the tenant equity vehicle. Denver7 reported in February 2026 that OEDIT describes its new renter rewards program as the tenant equity vehicle, and that the first property in it, Fall River Village in Estes Park, pays tenants who pay on time 2% of their rent back each month.

LIHTC conversion after year 15. Federal law lets an owner grant tenants, a resident management corporation, a qualified nonprofit or a government agency a right of first refusal to buy a tax credit building after the compliance period, at a minimum price set by its outstanding debt and taxes, without losing the credit. CHN Housing Partners in Cleveland runs a lease-purchase program in which families in tax credit homes can take title starting in year 16.
Limited-equity cooperatives, which also serve renters who become shareholders. No Colorado example was verified for this brief.

sections.heading: Colorado law and money
items: Proposition 123 equity program (C.R.S. 29-32-104; OEDIT contracts with an administrator, the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority, to run it): equity investments in low- and middle-income multifamily rental housing, with the tenant equity vehicle described above. For the 2026-27 state fiscal year, HB26-1360 sets the program shares by priority instead of the usual percentages: concessionary debt first, this equity program second, land banking third.

Proposition 123 land banking: grants to local governments and loans to nonprofits to acquire and preserve land for affordable housing, which is where a land trust or a deed-restricted ownership project can get its site.

Proposition 123 affordable home ownership program (run by DOLA's Division of Housing): down-payment assistance for first-time buyers, prioritising first-generation buyers, plus support for community land trusts and grants or loans to mobile home owners buying their park.

Mobile home park opportunity to purchase (C.R.S. 38-12-217): a landlord must give notice before selling a park; a group of home owners then has 120 days to submit a purchase offer and another 120 days to close, and the landlord must negotiate in good faith.
Mobile Home Park Resident Empowerment Loan and Grant Program (C.R.S. 24-32-728, created by SB22-160): acquisition and capital improvement financing for home owners buying their park.

Community land trust property tax exemption (HB23-1184, C.R.S. 39-3-127.7): from tax year 2024 the land a land trust holds for affordable homeownership can be exempt when it is a separate parcel from the house. The house itself is still taxed. No Colorado law was found that requires assessors to value a deed-restricted home at its restricted price.

sections.heading: What the evidence shows
paragraphs: The strongest studies are of established for-sale programs. They answer whether homes stay affordable and whether owners keep them. They answer less well how much wealth owners build compared with what they would have built otherwise, because none of them follows a matched group of market-rate buyers.

Resold homes stayed affordable to households well below the area median; few owners lost their home to foreclosure, and over 90 percent remained homeowners five years after buying in the three programs with data.
Its rate of return is on the buyer's down payment, not total wealth; it also finds that a formula giving sellers more return makes resale homes less affordable.

Land trust loans outperformed loans in the MBA national delinquency survey on every comparable delinquency and foreclosure measure; prime loans were 4.3 times more likely to be seriously delinquent at the end of 2009.
Self-reported survey of 42 land trusts during the foreclosure crisis; it also found only a minority of land trusts had outside funding to expand or support their work.

Owners still carry market risk: the typical owner had negative net appreciation during the recovery period.
Shared equity generally offers lower returns than market-rate ownership but can expose owners to far less risk.

briefs.title: Local workforce housing without tax credits: how Colorado resort towns house the people who work there
briefs.takeaway: Where second homes take a large share of the housing, tax-credit housing alone cannot house the people who work there: federal low-income housing tax credits are capped at an average of 60% of area median income, and resort economies need homes for workers above that line. Colorado's resort towns answer with local money, mostly lodging, short-term rental and sales taxes, spent on deed restrictions, town-owned rentals and seasonal beds. These programs reach households tax credits cannot. They cost local money, and in their lightest form they keep a home for a local worker without capping its price.
briefs.summary: The Census counts a home as seasonal, recreational or occasional-use when it is vacant most of the year; in resort towns that is mostly second homes and short-term rentals. By that count, more than 40% of the homes in the places listed below are held for occasional use. Federal law requires a tax-credit project to rent-restrict at least 20% of its units to households at 50% of area median income or below, or 40% at 60% or below, or keep the average designated limit at no more than 60%. The resort programs on record reach a wider band: the Aspen-Pitkin County Housing Authority's (APCHA) ownership categories run from below 50% AMI to 240% AMI, Breckenridge's Wellington neighborhood has income limits of 80% to 150% AMI, and Steamboat's Cottonwoods condos are open to incomes up to 140% AMI. Some set no income limit at all and require only that the occupant work locally. Since 2022 Colorado law has let county lodging taxes and local marketing district taxes pay for housing and child care for the tourism-related workforce, including seasonal workers.
briefs.implications: For a developer or a town, the choice is not tax credits or local programs; it is which households each one reaches. A tax-credit project brings federal equity and serves households at or below 60% AMI on average; the resort programs spend local money and reach the workers above that. Buying a deed restriction on an existing home adds a workforce home without construction, which is why Vail, Eagle County, Summit County, Breckenridge, Avon, Crested Butte and Steamboat Springs all run one. Read the restriction before counting the home as affordable: an occupancy-only restriction keeps the home for a local worker at market price, while a price-capped one also keeps it affordable to the next buyer. Payments, fees and income limits change every year, so check each program's current terms with the town before relying on a figure.

sections.heading: What Colorado law allows
items: HB22-1117, signed March 31, 2022, added housing and child care for the tourism-related workforce, including seasonal workers, and for other workers in the community to the purposes a county lodging tax and a local marketing district tax may fund.

When a county lodging tax is created or its uses are expanded after January 1, 2022, at least 10% of its revenue must still go to advertising and marketing local tourism; a marketing district must keep at least 10% for its pre-2022 purposes. The law sets no minimum share for housing.

A county lodging tax was capped at 2% until HB25-1247 (2025) let county voters raise it to as much as 6% in unincorporated areas. It does not apply inside a municipality that levies its own lodging tax, which is why most of the town taxes below are the town's own excise tax.
Any new tax or tax rate increase needs voter approval in advance under the Taxpayer's Bill of Rights, so every tax in the next section went to an election.
The Colorado Department of Revenue does not administer municipal lodging taxes; its DR 1003 table lists the lodging tax rates it does track.

sections.heading: Housing for seasonal workers
paragraphs: HB22-1117 names seasonal workers among the people lodging tax money can now house. Seasonal beds on record are few and small: Crested Butte's The Ruby is a former bed and breakfast the town bought for communal seasonal housing, APCHA offers winter seasonal rentals at three locations on a first-come, first-served basis, and Summit County has master-leased former hotels for long-term rooms for local workers, though the county's page does not confirm those leases continue.

sections.heading: Compared with tax-credit housing
items: Who it reaches. Tax-credit units are limited to households at 50% or 60% of area median income, or an average of no more than 60%. The resort programs reach up to 240% AMI, and several set no income limit.

Where the money comes from. Tax credits bring federal equity into a project. These programs spend local tax money: Vail's InDEED had funded $13,064,618 for 178 deed restrictions by the town's November 2025 summary.
Speed. A buy-down adds a workforce home at closing, without land or construction. Eagle County's Good Deeds pays 15% of the purchase price, up to $187,500.

Durability. Occupancy-only restrictions such as Vail InDEED, Mi Casa Avon and the light option of Summit County and Breckenridge Housing Helps keep the home for a local worker at market price. Price-capped restrictions keep it affordable to the next buyer as well: APCHA adds 3% simple appreciation a year, Chamonix Vail 1.5% a year and Smith Ranch 2% a year.

Local rules. Towns write their own requirements, such as Vail's rule that commercial development house 20% of the employees it generates, and Telluride's mitigation requirement of 40% to 90% depending on the use.
The two combine. APCHA manages 127 tax-credit units alongside its category housing, and Crested Butte's Mineral Point is tax-credit rental housing on land the town dedicated.
